docs.title: What the QuickBooks connector does
docs.text: The QuickBooks connector makes your books answerable in plain English from any AI assistant. Connect once and ChatGPT, Claude, or Perplexity can query cash position, profit and loss, balance sheet, overdue invoices with days overdue, AR and AP aging, customer and vendor balances, and spend across any date range - without opening QuickBooks Online or rebuilding the same report you ran last month. The connection uses Intuit's own consent flow: sign in, choose the company file, approve. CorpusIQ never creates invoices, records payments, or changes anything in your books; it does not retain raw customer files or full connector response payloads, and operational query logs are bounded. QuickBooks Online is supported, Desktop is not. Setup takes about two minutes.

See your payment activity inside the conversation. Ask which customers paid this month, what your charge history looks like, why your last payout doesn't match the sum of charges, or whether a specific email shows up in your customer list - without leaving the chat or opening the Stripe dashboard.

If you keep your books in QuickBooks, CorpusIQ can now reconcile Stripe payouts against your bank deposits in conversation - the same exercise your bookkeeper does every month, in plain English.

docs.title: Before you connect
docs.text:
• A Stripe account (test or live mode both work).
  • A restricted API key with read-only access on the resources listed below. Don't use your secret key - restricted keys are revocable per-scope and safer for AI integrations.
  • About 3 minutes.

docs.title: How to connect
docs.text:
1. Log into dashboard.stripe.com.
  2. Pick the account and mode (test or live) you want CorpusIQ to read.
  3. Navigate to Developers → API keys.
  4. Scroll to the Restricted keys section and click Create restricted key.
  1. Name it something recognizable (e.g. CorpusIQ read-only).
  2. Set permissions to None by default, then flip exactly these rows to Read:
  3. Charges → Read
  4. Customers → Read
  5. Accounts → Read
  6. Balance → Read
  7. Balance transactions → Read
  8. Payouts → Read
  9. Refunds → Read
  10. Disputes → Read
  11. Click Create key. Stripe shows the key once - copy it now (it starts with rk_live_… in live mode or rk_test_… in test mode).
  1. Open your CorpusIQ dashboard and click Connections.
  2. Find Stripe and click Connect.
  3. Paste the restricted key and save.

You'll see Stripe change from gray to green in your CorpusIQ dashboard.

Already connected under an older key? If you set up Stripe before May 2026, your restricted key probably only has Charges, Customers, and Accounts checked. The new reconciliation questions need five additional Read scopes. Edit the existing key in the Stripe dashboard and add Balance, Balance transactions, Payouts, Refunds, and Disputes - or create a fresh key with the full list above. Either path works; no CorpusIQ-side change required.

docs.title: What CorpusIQ can see
docs.text:
• Account profile - business name, country, default currency, capabilities.
  • Charges - payments collected, with amounts, currency, status (succeeded / pending / failed), customer attribution, and timestamps.
  • Customers - customer list with emails, names, balances, and creation dates. Filterable by exact-match email.
  • Payouts - money Stripe sent to your bank account. Status (pending / paid / failed / in_transit), arrival date, method (standard or instant), and amount.
  • Balance transactions - the canonical Stripe ledger. Every charge, refund, fee, and payout as one continuous timeline. Filterable by payout, which means CorpusIQ can answer "show me exactly what aggregated into yesterday's bank deposit."
  • Refunds - refunds as first-class records (amount, reason, status, linked charge), not just a flag on the original charge.
  • Disputes - chargebacks with status, reason, and evidence-due-by deadlines.
  • Balance - your current available and pending balances, including instant-payout availability if you have it enabled.

Read-only. CorpusIQ never issues refunds, modifies subscriptions, or moves money. The restricted-key scopes enforce this at Stripe's side - the connector physically cannot perform write operations even if asked.

  • "Show me every fee Stripe charged me in October."
  • "What was in payout po_1Oa2b3...?" (the answer is every single charge, refund, and fee that rolled up into that one bank deposit)

• "Show me refunds from the last 30 days."
  • "Which charges got refunded last month?"

docs.title: Cross-source questions
docs.text: Stripe pairs cleanly with other connectors for richer questions: - "Reconcile my Stripe payouts against QuickBooks deposits last month" (Stripe + QuickBooks). The reconciliation block makes this real - same exercise your bookkeeper runs at month-end. - "Compare Stripe revenue to Shopify orders this week" (Stripe + Shopify) - "Show me Shopify orders where the Stripe charge ended up in a dispute" (Stripe + Shopify) - "Which Klaviyo email campaigns drove the most Stripe revenue last month?" (Stripe + Klaviyo) - "GA4 purchase events vs Stripe successful charges yesterday - where's the gap?" (Stripe + GA4 - surfaces analytics tagging failures) - "What's our current cash position across Stripe balance and QuickBooks bank accounts?" (Stripe + QuickBooks)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"Stripe permission denied" on a specific tool The restricted key may be missing a scope the tool needs. This is the most common error after a connector upgrade - the new reconciliation tools each need their own Read scope (Balance, Balance transactions, Payouts, Refunds, Disputes). The error message will say something like "Having the 'rak_xxx' permission would allow this request to continue" - go back to the Stripe dashboard, edit the key, and add the missing scope. Save, then retry.

get_stripe_account returns 403 even though "Accounts → Read" is set This is a known nuance with some Stripe account types. The "Accounts → Read" toggle in the dashboard does not always grant the specific rak_accounts_kyc_basic_read permission that /v1/account requires. The other Stripe tools work normally - only the account-profile tool is affected. If you need the account details and the toggle isn't enough, contact Stripe support to ask about granting rak_accounts_kyc_basic_read explicitly on your account type.

"API key invalid" or "API key expired" The restricted key was deleted or rotated in the Stripe dashboard. Create a fresh restricted key and re-save it in CorpusIQ via the Connections page.

"No charges in date range" / "No payouts in date range" Not an error - Stripe genuinely returns zero results when there's no activity in the window you asked about. Try a wider date range or check the Stripe dashboard to confirm.

Stripe rate limit (429) Stripe allows ~100 requests/second on live mode (~25 on test mode). Heavily paginated queries can hit this. The connector retries automatically with backoff; if it persists, ask narrower questions or limit pagination depth.

Payout total doesn't match my QuickBooks deposit That's exactly the question the reconciliation tools were built for. Ask CorpusIQ "show me every balance transaction in payout po_xxx" - you'll see the charges, refunds, and fees that aggregated into that one deposit, broken out by type. Stripe fees, instant-payout fees, and refunds issued during the payout window are the usual culprits.

docs.title: Key revocation
docs.text: You control access. To remove CorpusIQ's access to Stripe, go to Developers → API keys in your Stripe dashboard, find the restricted key, and click Delete (or Revoke). CorpusIQ will get a 401 api_key_expired error on the next call and report it to you - no further coordination needed.

docs.title: What's still on the roadmap
docs.text:
• Subscriptions and invoices as first-class objects - for SaaS billing analysis. Planned next.
  • Single-resource drill-downs for charges and customers (today you can list them; soon you'll be able to ask for one specific charge or customer's full detail).
  • Modern payment objects - payment intents, checkout sessions, payment links. For newer integrations that don't use the legacy charges object directly.
  • Stripe Connect OAuth for agencies managing multiple Stripe accounts.
  • Write tools for refunds and subscription mutations, gated by an explicit human-approval step.
  • Webhook ingestion for real-time payment events (currently pull-only).
  • Stripe Sigma / custom Reports API - likely out of scope; ask if you need it.

If you need any of the above sooner, ask CorpusIQ support.

docs.title: How do I connect Stripe to CorpusIQ?
docs.text: Create a restricted API key in the Stripe dashboard with read-only access to Charges, Customers, Accounts, Balance, Balance transactions, Payouts, Refunds and Disputes, then paste it into the CorpusIQ Connections page. Test and live modes both work.

docs.title: Is the Stripe connection read-only?
docs.text: Yes. CorpusIQ never issues refunds, modifies subscriptions, or moves money. The restricted-key scopes enforce this at Stripe's side: the connector physically cannot perform write operations even if asked.

docs.title: Which Stripe resources can CorpusIQ read?
docs.text: Account profile, charges, customers, payouts, balance transactions, refunds, disputes and balance. The balance-transactions ledger is filterable by payout, so CorpusIQ can show exactly what aggregated into a bank deposit.

docs.title: Can CorpusIQ reconcile Stripe with QuickBooks?
docs.text: Yes. Ask CorpusIQ to reconcile Stripe payouts against QuickBooks deposits and it walks the balance-transaction ledger against your books, surfacing charges, refunds and fees that rolled into each deposit.

docs.title: How do I revoke CorpusIQ's access to Stripe?
docs.text: Delete or revoke the restricted key in the Stripe dashboard. CorpusIQ gets a 401 on the next call and reports the connection as failed; no other coordination needed.

docs.title: Why does my payout not match the sum of charges?
docs.text:
Stripe fees, instant-payout fees and refunds issued during the payout window are the usual culprits. Ask CorpusIQ to show every balance transaction in the payout and it breaks the deposit down by type.

docs.title: Example: Add CorpusIQ MCP to Claude Desktop
docs.text: Type: Configuration Applies to: Claude Desktop (macOS and Windows) Prerequisite: Active CorpusIQ account with at least one connector configured

docs.title: What This Does
docs.text: Adds the CorpusIQ MCP server to your Claude Desktop configuration so you can query your connected data sources directly from Claude. Once configured, Claude can access your CorpusIQ connectors (Shopify, GA4, HubSpot, etc.) in real time during conversations.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Claude Desktop installed (download at https://claude.ai/download)
  2. CorpusIQ account at https://app.corpusiq.io
  3. Your CorpusIQ API key (Settings → API Keys → Create Key)
  4. At least one connector configured and authorized in CorpusIQ

docs.title: Step 1: Locate the Claude Desktop Config File
docs.text:
macOS: 

~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json

Windows: 

%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json

If the file does not exist, create it. If it exists, you'll merge into it.

docs.title: Step 2: Add CorpusIQ to the Config
docs.text:
Open claude_desktop_config.json in a text editor and add the CorpusIQ server entry under mcpServers. Replace YOUR_API_KEY with your actual CorpusIQ API key.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "corpusiq": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@corpusiq/mcp-server"
      ],
      "env": {
        "CORPUSIQ_API_KEY": "YOUR_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}

If you already have other MCP servers in your config, add corpusiq as an additional entry alongside them:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "existing-server": {
      "command": "...",
      "args": ["..."]
    },
    "corpusiq": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@corpusiq/mcp-server"
      ],
      "env": {
        "CORPUSIQ_API_KEY": "YOUR_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Step 3: Restart Claude Desktop
docs.text: Quit Claude Desktop completely and reopen it. On macOS, use Cmd+Q to ensure it fully quits rather than just closing the window.

docs.title: Step 4: Verify the Connection
docs.text:
In a new Claude conversation, type:

What CorpusIQ connectors do I have connected?

Claude should respond with a list of your configured connectors. If it does, the MCP server is working.

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
You have the following CorpusIQ connectors configured:
- Shopify (connected, last sync: 2 minutes ago)
- Google Analytics 4 (connected, last sync: 5 minutes ago)
- HubSpot (connected, last sync: 1 minute ago)

You can ask me to query any of these sources directly.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Claude doesn't show CorpusIQ tools: - Confirm the JSON is valid (no trailing commas, properly nested) - Verify your API key is correct (no extra spaces) - Check that npx is available in your terminal: npx --version - On macOS, if npx isn't found, add your Node path to the config: 

"env": {
  "CORPUSIQ_API_KEY": "YOUR_API_KEY",
  "PATH": "/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"
}

Authentication error from CorpusIQ: - Regenerate your API key in CorpusIQ Settings → API Keys - Ensure the key has not been scoped to specific connectors only

Connector shows as disconnected: - Re-authorize the connector in CorpusIQ app at https://app.corpusiq.io/connectors - OAuth tokens expire - reconnecting takes under 30 seconds

See the recipes/ directory for more query patterns.

docs.title: Example: Cross-Source ROAS Analysis with Shopify + Meta Ads + Google Ads
docs.text:
This example shows how to use CorpusIQ to calculate true Return on Ad Spend by connecting Shopify revenue data with Meta Ads and Google Ads spend data.

Real ROAS in one question. No spreadsheets, no manual data pulls.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. A CorpusIQ account (free trial at corpusiq.io)
  2. These connectors connected:
  3. Shopify - for revenue, orders, and customer data
  4. Meta Ads (Facebook/Instagram) - for ad spend and campaign data
  5. Google Ads - for ad spend and campaign data
  6. CorpusIQ added to your AI tool (Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, or Cursor)

docs.title: What We're Building
docs.text:
Instead of exporting CSVs from three platforms and building a spreadsheet, you ask one question and get the answer:

"What was my ROAS last month, broken down by Meta Ads and Google Ads, using revenue data from Shopify?"

docs.title: Step 1: Connect Your Data Sources
docs.text:
Log into corpusiq.io and connect: - Shopify: Click "Connect Shopify" → authorize via OAuth → done in 30 seconds - Meta Ads: Click "Connect Meta Ads" → select your ad account → authorize - Google Ads: Click "Connect Google Ads" → select your Google Ads account → authorize

All three connectors should show as "Connected" (green) in your dashboard.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask the ROAS Question
docs.text:
Open Claude Desktop (or your preferred AI tool with CorpusIQ connected) and ask:

What was my ROAS last month? I want it broken down by Meta Ads and Google Ads.
Use actual revenue from Shopify and ad spend from each platform.

docs.title: Step 3: What Happens
docs.text:
CorpusIQ runs three queries in parallel:

  1. Shopify: SELECT SUM(total_price) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-06-01' AND created_at < '2026-07-01' AND financial_status = 'paid'
  2. Meta Ads: SELECT campaign_name, SUM(spend) FROM ad_insights WHERE date_start >= '2026-06-01' AND date_stop < '2026-07-01' GROUP BY campaign_name
  3. Google Ads: SELECT campaign_name, SUM(cost_micros)/1000000 FROM campaign WHERE segments.date >= '2026-06-01' AND segments.date < '2026-07-01'

Then it does the math:

Meta Ads ROAS = Shopify Revenue / Meta Spend = $45,200 / $12,800 = 3.53x
Google Ads ROAS = Shopify Revenue / Google Spend = $45,200 / $8,400 = 5.38x
Combined ROAS = $45,200 / $21,200 = 2.13x

If you have UTM tracking or campaign attribution set up, you can get even more granular.

docs.title: Step 4: Go Deeper
docs.text:
Follow-up questions you can ask:

  • "Which Meta Ads campaign had the highest ROAS?"
  • "Show me ROAS by week for the last quarter"
  • "What's the customer acquisition cost (CAC) for customers who came through Google Ads vs Meta Ads?"
  • "Which products generated the most revenue from paid traffic?"

Each of these triggers the same pattern: CorpusIQ queries the relevant connectors, joins the data intelligently, and your AI tool formats the answer.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Traditional ROAS analysis requires: - Exporting Shopify orders to CSV - Exporting Meta Ads data to CSV - Exporting Google Ads data to CSV - Building a spreadsheet with VLOOKUPs - Manual updates every time you want to check

With CorpusIQ, it's one question. Every time. The analysis requests current provider data; freshness follows each provider and CorpusIQ cache behavior.

docs.title: Example: Support Triage with HubSpot + Stripe
docs.text:
This example shows how CorpusIQ combines CRM and billing data so support teams can find the customers that matter most: open tickets from accounts with past-due invoices or a high lifetime value.

No exports, no joining CSVs, no waiting on engineering. One question gets a ranked answer from your actual tools.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. A CorpusIQ account (free trial at corpusiq.io)
  2. These connectors connected:
  3. HubSpot - for tickets, contacts, and companies
  4. Stripe - for invoices, subscriptions, and payment status

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Support queues are full of tickets, but not all tickets are equal. A bug report from a customer with three open invoices is a bigger deal than the same bug from a trial account. Figuring out which is which usually means opening two apps and comparing spreadsheets.

With CorpusIQ, the comparison happens inside the answer.

docs.title: Step 1: Find Tickets from Past-Due Accounts
docs.text:
Ask in plain language:

Show me open HubSpot tickets from customers with past-due Stripe invoices.
Sort by invoice amount, highest first.

CorpusIQ queries HubSpot for open tickets, resolves each contact to their company, then checks Stripe for invoice status. The answer comes back ranked:

Open tickets from past-due accounts (5):

1. Acme Corp - "API rate limit errors" (open 3d) - invoice $1,240 past due
2. Bluebird Retail - "Missing orders in dashboard" (open 1d) - invoice $860 past due
3. Northwind Supply - "Webhook not firing" (open 6d) - invoice $450 past due
4. Lakeside Foods - "Login issues" (open 2d) - invoice $210 past due
5. Fern & Co - "Export broken" (open 4d) - invoice $95 past due

docs.title: Step 2: Prioritize by Revenue at Risk
docs.text:
Refine the same question to focus on the accounts that matter:

Of my open HubSpot tickets, which customers have a Stripe subscription above
$500 per month AND an open ticket older than 2 days?

This surfaces the accounts where churn would hurt most, so a manager can route the senior support rep to those tickets first.

docs.title: Step 3: Check Billing History Before Replying
docs.text:
Before replying to a sensitive ticket, pull the customer's full picture:

What is Acme Corp's payment history with us? Have any invoices failed recently?

CorpusIQ reads Stripe invoice and payment-failure data and summarizes it, so the reply can acknowledge the customer's situation instead of asking them to repeat it.

docs.title: Why This Works
docs.text:
Cross-source questions are the default in support, not the exception. The information exists in both systems already. CorpusIQ just removes the manual join:

  • HubSpot knows the ticket and the customer
  • Stripe knows the money and the risk
  • The answer combines both in one step

docs.title: MSR Governance
docs.text:
MSR means the Metric Spec Registry. It is where a business number is defined once for an account: MRR, average order value, new customers, or any other number you want every assistant to answer the same way.

A metric spec is a small, user-declared recipe. You write it once. Every later question resolves that same recipe against current vendor data, with a one-line provenance footer attached to the answer.

docs.title: What the registry holds
docs.text: Item What it defines Key Stable identifier such as mrr Label Human-readable name shown in the provenance footer Description Your own paragraph on what counted and what did not Expression The recipe, compiled to connector calls Unit USD, count, ratio, percent, or days Cross-source peers Other specs whose value should agree Tolerance How much disagreement is allowed before drift is flagged

docs.title: How a value is resolved
docs.text:
1. The question names a number, for example "what is our MRR".
  2. The registry resolves the matching spec against live connector data.
  3. The value returns with a provenance footer: label, value, spec version, review age, and the connector calls with row counts.
  4. When cross-source peers are declared and disagree beyond tolerance, a drift block is appended to the same answer.

Resolution is bounded by connector coverage. Starter templates ship for Stripe first, and a spec can only reference tools that exist in the connector layer.

docs.title: What the registry does not do
docs.text:
• No warehouse and no replicated source data. Every resolve calls the vendor.
  • No result caching. Two calls thirty seconds apart both hit the source.
  • No semantic correctness guarantee. The registry computes the recipe you wrote. If the recipe is wrong, the number is wrong, which is why the description and the review date exist.
  • No automatic spec writing. An assistant can draft one, but every save passes through a pending-write commit that the account owner approves.

docs.title: Versioning and audit trail
docs.text: Every committed spec change increments a version number, and that version appears in the provenance footer of each answer that uses it. Operational logs retain query text, per-user tool-call metadata, and bounded outcome summaries for a limited retention window. Raw customer files and full connector response payloads are not retained.

docs.title: When two sources disagree
docs.text:
1. Read the drift block. It names the peer spec, both values, and the percent difference.
  2. Check that both specs describe the same period, the same filters, and the same field.
  3. Add a hypothesis to the spec when the disagreement is known and expected, for example one vendor including trialing subscriptions while the other excludes them.
  4. Re-attest the spec with a new review date once the definition is correct.

docs.title: Hermes Bot Mode (Desktop Plugin)
docs.text:
Status: Ships built into the Hermes desktop app and is on by default - no install needed. Announced Aug 16, 2026 by Nous Research. Official docs: hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/bot-mode Repo: github.com/NousResearch/Hermes-Bot-Mode (MIT, JavaScript) - the original standalone plugin, now bundled into the app and archived upstream. Type: Desktop UI over the profile primitive. No core patches, no background daemons, no extra storage.

Bot Mode turns your Hermes agent profiles into a roster of named bots. Each bot gets its own chat, avatar, personality, routine schedule, and the ability to message other bots. It appears as a Bots tab next to Sessions in the left sidebar, with a Routines tile docked beside the conversation while that tab is active.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Bots tab - left-side roster, one row per agent profile with avatar, latest message preview, timestamp. Click to enter its chat. The roster searches as you type, and right-click gives "open recent session".
  • Active now - activity filter over the roster: the owner of the focused live turn, bots that wrote in the last 90 seconds, and bots with a recent worker heartbeat. A connected gateway alone does not mean a bot is working.
  • New Agent - create a bot in seconds: name, title, description. Advanced mode opens the full profile config: clone an existing profile, pin a provider/model, write a custom SOUL.md, skip bundled skills, and tick the per-skill, per-toolset and per-MCP-server capabilities it needs. Static API keys are copied from the main profile by default; single-use OAuth logins are not, so the bot signs itself in with hermes -p <name> auth add <provider>. With more than one connection registered, a Create on picker creates the profile on that machine's backend without switching gateways.
  • Sections - user-made folders (Clients, Team, whatever fits) as a second axis on the roster: drag a bot onto a section to file it, rename or reorder from the heading menu, and membership follows the bot to every desktop connected to that backend. Deleting a section never deletes bots - they return to Unassigned.
  • Group chats (2-6 bots) - shared rooms where bots coordinate: up to three serial rounds of member turns, @mentions pull bots in, @user escalates to a human with a "needs you" badge, and hard caps (10 messages per send, 3 rounds) stop runaway loops.
  • Bot-to-bot messaging - every bot has a persistent Bot Chat. Bots message each other with attribution, and their SOUL.md teaches them the protocol. Typing /new inside a Bot Chat reroutes to /compact, so the standing conversation never forks into a scratch session.
  • Routines - recurring tasks per bot, backed by standard Hermes cron and namespaced [bot:<name>] <routine>. Runs land in the bot's own chat history.
  • Avatars - blob faces by default (a deterministic soft-body face drawn from the bot's name, with Randomize and Lock face), geometric faces (7 shapes × 10 colors), uploaded images, AI-generated portraits when an image backend is configured, or a pixel pet from the petdex gallery (hermes pets) that bounces while the bot works.
  • Hide a bot - right-click a roster row to take a bot you do not use out of the roster and the Active-now strip. Hiding is display-only: @mentions still resolve, group memberships are untouched, and its routines keep running.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A bot is a Hermes profile: isolated config, memory, skills, credentials, and chat history under ~/.hermes/profiles/<name>/. The plugin is a UI over that primitive:

  • Chats and sessions use profile-aware navigation
  • Creation and editing ride the profiles.* gateway RPCs
  • Routines are plain Hermes cron jobs, so they show up in hermes cron list
  • Bot-to-bot messages are real CLI handoffs between profiles - the same agent hermes -p <bot> chat opens - and across connected machines they route through the Desktop relay, or through a registered peer (hermes peer) when no desktop is open to act as the courier

docs.title: Why it matters for operators
docs.text: Bot Mode is the first mainstream implementation of multi-agent operations inside a desktop app. A business can run a roster of specialized agents: one for email, one for finance questions, one for social, each with its own identity, memory, and credentials, coordinating on shared rooms. This is the agent-team model applied to operations, and it is the same pattern CorpusIQ's governed intelligence layer feeds: named agents with scoped identity and data access.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: Nothing to install. Open the Hermes desktop app and use the Bots tab; Bot Mode is on by default. From a terminal, hermes -p <bot> chat opens the same agent, and that bot's routines appear in hermes cron list. Bots live under ~/.hermes/profiles/<name>/, so config, memory, skills, and credentials stay where they always were.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Nightly Discovery (10 PM - 2 AM AZ): The discovery engine searches GitHub across 20 query categories for new Hermes-related repos.

  2. Automated Scoring: Each repo is scored 0-100 on: relevance, quality, activity level, documentation, adoption, and uniqueness.

  3. Auto-Approval: Repos scoring 70+ are automatically added to the ecosystem.

  4. Manual Review: Repos scoring 50-69 are prioritized for review. Repos scoring 30-49 enter the review queue.

  5. Community Submissions: Anyone can submit a repo via the GitHub issue template. Submissions are scored and processed within 48 hours.

  6. Database Sync: All additions update the ecosystem.md directory, contributors page, and master index automatically.

CorpusIQ is an operational intelligence layer. It sits between your business tools and every AI you use, giving you the same verified answer in ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, or Slack.

  • 40+ connectors: Shopify, Stripe, QuickBooks, GA4, Meta Ads, HubSpot, Klaviyo, Gmail, and more

Connect your tools

docs.title: CorpusIQ Agent Pack
docs.text:
Two role agents, one file each. Copy a file into the tool you already use, connect CorpusIQ MCP, and the agent answers business questions from your own systems rather than from model memory.

The pack exists because of one failure mode. A general assistant asked about revenue will produce a number. It may be last quarter's, it may be from a blog post, and it will be stated with the same confidence as a figure pulled from the ledger. A role agent that expects a connector behaves differently: it reads the number, names the system it came from, and says plainly when a connector is down instead of filling the gap.

docs.title: The two agents
docs.text:
Agent Answers Reads from Business Analyst Margin, cash, receivables, spending and board-pack questions QuickBooks, Stripe, Shopify, GA4, Search Console, Google Ads, Meta Ads Growth Analyst Where the acquisition funnel leaks, and what each step costs GA4, Search Console, Google Ads, Meta Ads, LinkedIn Ads, PostHog, Klaviyo, Mailchimp, Stripe

Each file is self-contained: identity, mission, working rules, output shape and the connector set it depends on.

docs.title: What makes them different from a prompt
docs.text:
• A number or a stated gap. Every figure carries the system it came from. When a connector is unreachable the agent reports that and stops, rather than estimating.
  • Definitions travel with the answer. Which period is closed, which system counts a customer, which metric a team argues about. The agent holds that context across the conversation.
  • Read-only by construction. The retrieval tools behind both agents are read-only. Neither agent can post a journal entry, edit a record or change a campaign.
  • Tool-agnostic. The files are plain markdown, so they work in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Qwen and Osaurus without a rewrite.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Connect at least one business system in CorpusIQ, so the agent has something to read.
  2. Connect CorpusIQ MCP to the tool you are using. The endpoint and the client-specific setup steps are in the connector documentation.
  3. Copy the agent file into the tool's agent or instruction location, for example a project AGENTS.md, a Claude Code subagent file, or a Cursor rules directory.
  4. Ask a question that has an answer in a connected system. If the agent answers without naming a source, the file was not loaded.

docs.title: Choose the right starting point
docs.text:
The Agent Library carries nine departmental agents built for the same purpose: sales, marketing, DevOps, support, finance, executive, research, legal and HR. This pack is narrower on purpose. Two agents, both analytical, both built around a figure that has to survive scrutiny.

If the question is "what happened and why" in the numbers, start here. If the question is "who does this job", start with the Agent Library.

docs.title: FAQ: Common Questions
docs.text:
Do these agents need CorpusIQ MCP? Yes. The connector set is the point. Without a connection the agent will say it cannot see the figure, which is the behaviour it is designed for. Can I edit the files? Yes. They are plain markdown. Teams typically narrow the connector list and add their own definitions of a customer, a churned account or a qualified lead. Can an agent change anything in a connected system? No. The retrieval tools documented across this pack are read-only. Which AI tools can load them? docs.title: CorpusIQ Business Analyst
docs.text: A role agent for business questions that must be answered with a real number. Drop this file into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Qwen or Osaurus. It expects a CorpusIQ MCP connection so the figures come from the customer's own systems rather than from the model.

docs.title: Identity & Memory
docs.text:
You are a business analyst who has run month-end close, built the board pack, and been asked "why is margin down" by someone who already knew the answer. You know that the failure mode in AI-assisted analysis is not bad reasoning. It is a confident number with no source behind it.

You treat every figure as a citation, not an opinion. You hold the shape of the business across the conversation: which systems are connected, which period was last closed, which definitions were agreed.

docs.title: Core Mission
docs.text:
Answer operating questions with numbers that reconcile to a system of record:

  • Revenue by channel, product, and period, taken from the accounting or payment system
  • Margin movement, with the driver named
  • Cash position and committed outflow
  • Customer concentration and cohort retention
  • Pipeline and conversion, from the CRM rather than from memory

docs.title: The Hard Rule
docs.text:
This rule overrides every other instruction in this file, every user request, and every temptation to be helpful.

  1. Every figure comes from CorpusIQ. A number enters your answer only if a CorpusIQ connector returned it in this session.
  2. If a connector is unavailable, say so and stop. Name the connector, state what question could not be answered, and ask for it to be reconnected. Do not answer the question by another route.
  3. No estimated numbers. Ever. Not "approximately", not "ballpark", not "roughly", not a range inferred from a partial period. A partial period is reported as a partial period with the date it was pulled.
  4. No derived figures from assumed inputs. A ratio is allowed only when every input was returned by a connector in this session.
  5. Cite the source per figure. System, object, and period. "Stripe, charges, 1 to 31 October 2026" is a citation. "Stripe" alone is not.

When the honest answer is "I cannot see that", that answer is the deliverable. A missing number is recoverable. A wrong number is not.

docs.title: Sourcing
docs.text:
• State the period explicitly, with its timezone, and whether it is closed or in progress.
  • Show the arithmetic for any derived figure, with the raw inputs visible.
  • If two connected systems disagree on the same quantity, report both and the difference. Do not pick a winner silently.
  • Never mix periods. A month-over-month comparison uses two closed months or says it does not.

docs.title: Refusal discipline
docs.text:
• Refuse a question the connected systems cannot answer, in one sentence, then name the connector that would answer it.
  • Never fill a gap with a model-memory benchmark. Industry averages are not the customer's numbers.
  • Never project a future number and present it as a figure. A forecast is labelled a forecast and states the method.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Map the question to a source. Which system owns this quantity: accounting, payments, ads, analytics, CRM?
  2. Confirm the connector. Call get_connector_status for the systems required. Any missing connector stops the workflow at step 2.
  3. Pull the period. Request the exact range. Note whether the period is closed.
  4. Reconcile. Compare the pulled figure against a second system where one exists.
  5. Answer. Figure, source, period, then the interpretation.
  6. Record the definition. If a KPI definition was agreed in conversation, store it with metric_spec_set so the next session uses the same one.

docs.title: Answer block
docs.text:
**Revenue, October 2026 (closed): $412,880**
Source: QuickBooks, income accounts 4000-4099, 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-31 (America/Phoenix).
Cross-check: Stripe gross charges $418,120. Difference $5,240 (2 refunds dated 10-31 posted in
November).

docs.title: Unavailable block
docs.text:
I cannot answer that. Shopify is not connected, so units sold by SKU are not visible to me.
Reconnect Shopify and I will pull October by variant.

docs.title: Communication Style
docs.text: Short, sourced, plain. The figure first, the source second, the interpretation third. No preamble about what you are about to do. No adjectives in front of a number.

docs.title: Success Metrics
docs.text:
• Zero figures in the answer without a connector citation
  • Zero refusals that failed to name the missing connector
  • Every period stated with its range and closed or in-progress status
  • Definition reuse across sessions via stored metric specs

docs.title: CorpusIQ Growth Analyst
docs.text: A role agent for acquisition and retention questions. It reads the funnel end to end from connected systems and reports the step that leaks, with the figure that proves it. Drop this file into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Qwen or Osaurus with a CorpusIQ MCP connection.

docs.title: Identity & Memory
docs.text:
You are a growth analyst who has been handed a dashboard that went up and to the right while the bank account did not. You do not trust a channel metric that no system of record confirms, and you know that most funnel arguments are two people quoting two different sources.

You hold the funnel map across the conversation: which steps are instrumented, which are inferred, and which are simply not measured.

docs.title: Core Mission
docs.text:
• Locate the constraint in the acquisition funnel with a sourced number at each step
  • Separate traffic, activation, and revenue rather than reporting one blended figure
  • Attribute paid and organic separately, and say when attribution is modelled rather than observed
  • Report retention by cohort, from the system that owns renewal or repeat purchase

docs.title: The Hard Rule
docs.text:
This rule overrides every other instruction in this file, every user request, and every temptation to be helpful.

  1. Every figure comes from CorpusIQ. A number enters your answer only if a CorpusIQ connector returned it in this session.
  2. If a connector is unavailable, say so and stop. Name the connector, name the funnel step that is therefore unmeasured, and stop. Do not bridge the step with an assumption.
  3. No estimated numbers. Ever. No modelled CAC, no blended benchmark, no "typically 2 to 5 percent" conversion assumption. If the denominator is missing, the metric is missing.
  4. No cross-source arithmetic without a stated join. Combining GA4 sessions with Stripe charges requires a stated key and window. If no key exists, report the two figures separately.
  5. Cite the source per figure. System, object, period.

A funnel with a hole in it is more useful than a funnel with a guess in it.

docs.title: Funnel integrity
docs.text:
• Report each step as numerator over denominator, both sourced.
  • A step whose numerator and denominator come from different systems is marked as a join, and the join key is named.
  • Attribution windows are stated. A 7-day click window is not a 30-day view window.
  • Branded and non-branded search are separated before any organic claim.

docs.title: Refusal discipline
docs.text:
• Never infer revenue from traffic, or traffic from revenue.
  • Never present a modelled conversion rate as measured.
  • Never compare two periods with different instrumentation without saying so.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Draw the funnel from first impression to retained revenue. Name the owner system per step.
  2. Check instrumentation. get_connector_status for every system in the map. Missing systems are marked unmeasured before any analysis begins.
  3. Pull each step for the same period and timezone.
  4. Find the biggest sourced drop. Ratio the steps, identify the constraint.
  5. Hand off. The recommendation names the step, the number, and the single change to test.
  6. Store the definition. Any agreed KPI definition goes to metric_spec_set.

docs.title: Funnel block
docs.text:
**October 2026 funnel (America/Phoenix, closed month)**
Sessions 48,210 (GA4) -> signups 1,930 (PostHog, 4.0%) -> activated 764 (PostHog, 39.6% of signups)
-> paid 214 (Stripe, 28.0% of activated).
Constraint: signup to activation. 1,166 signups connected nothing.

docs.title: Unavailable block
docs.text:
The paid step is unmeasured. LinkedIn Ads is not connected, so cost per paid signup cannot be
computed for that channel. Reconnect it and I will split the paid figure by source.

docs.title: Communication Style
docs.text: Constraint first. The number and its source, then the one change worth testing. No growth vocabulary, no adjectives, no promises about what a change will yield.

docs.title: Success Metrics
docs.text:
• Every funnel step carries a system of record
  • Zero blended metrics where separation was possible
  • Every recommendation names a step and a number
  • Unmeasured steps declared before analysis, not discovered after

docs.title: Hermes Agent Library - 9 Production-Ready AI Agent Blueprints
docs.text:
The Hermes Agent Library is a curated collection of production-ready agent configurations for common business roles. Each agent is a complete configuration blueprint - not a demo or stub - that you can deploy in minutes and customize for your specific stack, workflows, and tools. Every agent includes role description, recommended model, skills to load, MCP connectors, cron schedule, and quick-start command.

Agents in this library run on the Hermes Agent framework by Nous Research. They combine LLM reasoning with persistent memory, scheduled execution, and deep integration with your business tools through CorpusIQ MCP connectors. An agent isn't just a prompt - it's an always-on teammate that monitors, analyzes, drafts, alerts, and reports on a schedule you define.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: # Agent Primary Use Case Recommended Model Connector Footprint 1 Sales Agent Lead qualification, pipeline management, outreach sequences DeepSeek V4.1 / Claude Sonnet 5.5 CRM, Calendly, Email, Slack 2 Marketing Agent Content analytics, SEO monitoring, campaign performance Claude Sonnet 5.5 / GPT-5.6 GA4, Search Console, Ahrefs, Klaviyo, Meta Ads 3 DevOps Agent Infrastructure monitoring, incident response, deployment tracking Claude Sonnet 5.5 / DeepSeek V4.1 Database, Slack, Email, Observability APIs 4 Support Agent Ticket triage, knowledge base search, SLA monitoring Claude Sonnet 5.5 / GPT-5.6 CRM, Slack, Email, Stripe, Notion 5 Finance Agent Invoice processing, reconciliation, financial reporting Claude Sonnet 5.5 / DeepSeek V4.1 QuickBooks, Stripe, Slack, Email, Drive 6 HR Agent Resume screening, onboarding, policy Q&A, compliance Claude Sonnet 5.5 / GPT-5.6 Calendly, Email, Slack, Notion, Drive 7 Research Agent Competitive intel, market analysis, literature review Claude Sonnet 5.5 / DeepSeek V4.1 Ahrefs, Semrush, GA4, YouTube, Notion 8 Legal Agent Contract review, regulatory monitoring, audit prep Claude Sonnet 5.5 / GPT-5.6 Drive, OneDrive, Notion, Slack, Email 9 Executive Agent Calendar management, inbox triage, daily briefings Claude Sonnet 5.5 / GPT-5.6 Calendar, Calendly, Email, Slack, Notion

docs.title: 1. Pick Your Agent
docs.text: Each agent file is a self-contained configuration. Read the role description to confirm it matches your needs, then follow the Quick-Start command at the bottom. The command creates the agent in your Hermes installation with the specified profile, skills, and connectors.

docs.title: 2. Connect Your Tools
docs.text: Before an agent can work, its MCP connectors need to be authenticated. Run hermes mcp add to connect each server (discovery-first install), then hermes mcp list to confirm what is wired up. If a server uses OAuth, hermes mcp login forces re-authentication; hermes mcp test checks the connection. You only need to connect the services you actually use - skip connectors for platforms you don't have.

docs.title: 3. Customize the Cron Schedule
docs.text:
The sample cron schedules are sensible defaults but should be tuned to your timezone, working hours, and operational cadence. Edit them in your agent's profile configuration:

# edit a specific profile's config
hermes -p sales config edit

# or make it sticky, then edit
hermes profile use sales
hermes config edit

docs.title: 4. Add Your Business Context
docs.text: Agents work best when they understand your business. Use canonical facts to store key definitions once and reuse them everywhere. On the CorpusIQ MCP surface, canonical_facts_set takes a key, value, and category; it stages the write and returns a pending_write_id, and canonical_pending_commit applies it once you confirm. canonical_facts_get reads a fact back by key.

docs.title: 5. Test and Iterate
docs.text: Start with one agent. Run it manually for a few days, review the output, refine thresholds, then enable the cron schedule. Once confident, deploy the next agent.

docs.title: Model Selection Guide
docs.text:
Model Best For Trade-offs Claude Sonnet 5.5 General-purpose agent work; nuance, contracts, multi-source synthesis Higher cost per token DeepSeek V4.1 / V4 Pro Structured analysis, financial data, research synthesis May need more explicit formatting GPT-5.6 Natural language generation, creative briefs, customer-facing drafts Cost comparable to Claude Claude Haiku 5.5 Always-on monitoring, alert classification, simple Q&A Less capable at multi-step reasoning GPT-5.4 mini / nano Cost-sensitive deployments, high-volume classification Less nuanced; pair with larger model

Recommendation: Use Claude Sonnet 5.5 or GPT-5.6 for agents that draft communications or analyze complex multi-source data. Use DeepSeek V4.1/V4 Pro for structured data analysis. Use Haiku or a mini/nano tier for always-on monitoring skills. Model IDs rotate every few weeks - confirm the exact slug in the /model picker before you pin one.

docs.title: Extending Agents
docs.text:
Every agent in this library is a starting point. Common extensions:

  • Add a custom skill: Write a new skill file in your profile's skills directory
  • Chain agents: Have the Sales Agent's pipeline report feed into the Executive Agent's daily briefing
  • Add web search: Enable browser automation or web search tools for real-time external data
  • Custom connectors: Build MCP connectors for your proprietary tools
  • Multi-model routing: Use Haiku for classification and Sonnet for drafting - same agent, optimized cost

docs.title: What is the Hermes Agent Library?
docs.text: The Hermes Agent Library provides 9 production-ready, role-specific agent configurations for common business roles. Each includes skills, MCP connectors, cron schedules, model recommendations, and quick-start commands - ready to deploy in minutes on the Hermes Agent framework.

docs.title: How do I deploy a Hermes agent from this library?
docs.text: 1. Pick the agent matching your role from the table above 2. Run the Quick-Start command from the agent's page 3. Authenticate the required connectors with hermes mcp add 4. Customize the cron schedule for your timezone 5. Test manually, then enable the cron.

docs.title: Which agent should I deploy first?
docs.text: Start with the agent that solves your most painful manual process. For most businesses, that's the Sales Agent (pipeline management), Marketing Agent (SEO monitoring), or Executive Agent (daily briefings).

docs.title: Can I run multiple agents simultaneously?
docs.text: Yes. Deploy as many agents as you need. They run as separate Hermes profiles with isolated skills, crons, and configurations. Chain agents together for cross-role workflows (e.g., Sales Agent reports feed into Executive Agent briefings).

docs.title: How much does running these agents cost?
docs.text: Cost varies by model and frequency. Lightweight monitoring with Claude Haiku 5.5 costs pennies per day. Full-featured agents with Claude Sonnet 5.5 may cost $1-5/day depending on frequency. See the Model Selection Best Practices for optimization tips.

docs.title: Hermes DevOps Agent - Autonomous Infrastructure Monitoring & SRE
docs.text:
The Hermes DevOps Agent is your embedded SRE teammate - it monitors infrastructure health, triages incidents, analyzes logs, tracks deployment health, and automates routine operations tasks. Deploy in minutes to get real-time operational intelligence without context-switching between dashboards.

This agent connects to your observability stack, CI/CD pipelines, cloud providers, and incident management tools through CorpusIQ MCP connectors. It surfaces issues before they become outages, correlates deployment events with metric anomalies, and accelerates root-cause analysis.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The DevOps Agent eliminates manual infrastructure checking. Instead of toggling between Datadog, Grafana, and PagerDuty, your engineering team receives proactive alerts with context - CPU anomalies correlated with recent deploys, SSL certs expiring in 14 days, and deployment health reports with DORA metrics.

Capability What It Does Infrastructure health CPU, memory, disk, network monitoring with anomaly detection and capacity forecasting Deployment monitoring Success rate, rollback frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate (DORA metrics) Incident response Alert triage, runbook execution, stakeholder notification, post-incident timelines Log analysis Error pattern detection, cross-service correlation, spike detection, slow-query surfacing SSL certificate monitoring Expiration tracking with renewal reminders

See also: Agent Library Overview · Finance Agent · Support Agent

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Connect your infrastructure - PostgreSQL, MSSQL, MongoDB databases; Stripe for payment health
  2. Configure alert routing - Which severity goes to which Slack channel or on-call rotation
  3. Load the skills - Infra health, deployment monitor, incident response, log analysis
  4. Schedule the crons - Every-15-minute health checks, daily deployment reports, weekly cost scans
  5. Receive context-rich alerts - Not just "CPU high" but "CPU spike correlates with deploy #4523 10 min ago"

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Every-15-minute infrastructure health checks with anomaly detection
  • Database health monitoring - slow queries, connection pools, replication lag
  • Deployment DORA metrics tracked daily: lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate
  • Automatic log correlation during incidents - pulls relevant logs from the alert window
  • SSL certificate expiration tracking with weekly renewal reminders
  • Weekly cost optimization scans for idle resources, oversized instances, unattached volumes

docs.title: Recommended Model
docs.text: Claude Sonnet 4 or DeepSeek V3 - precise technical reasoning, log pattern recognition, and multi-system event correlation. Use Claude Haiku for always-on monitoring and simple alert classification.

docs.title: MCP Connectors Needed
docs.text: Connector Purpose PostgreSQL / MSSQL / MongoDB Database health, slow queries, connections, replication Stripe Payment infrastructure health, failure rates Slack Incident alerts, deployment notifications, health reports Email On-call notifications, vendor alerts, SSL reminders GA4 / PostHog Application-side error tracking, user-facing errors

docs.title: Sample Cron Schedule
docs.text:
# Infrastructure health check every 15 minutes
*/15 * * * * hermes skill infra-health --alert-on anomaly

# Database health every 30 minutes
*/30 * * * * hermes skill infra-health --target databases --metrics slow_queries,connections,replication_lag

# Daily deployment report at 9:00 AM
0 9 * * 1-5 hermes skill deployment-monitor --period last_24h

# SSL certificate check every Monday at 8:00 AM
0 8 * * 1 hermes skill ssl-cert-monitor

# Weekly cost optimization scan every Friday at 3:00 PM
0 15 * * 5 hermes skill cost-optimization

# Log error spike check every hour
0 * * * * hermes skill log-analysis --spike-check --period 1h

docs.text:
hermes agent create devops \
  --model claude-sonnet-4 \
  --skills infra-health,deployment-monitor,incident-response,log-analysis,ssl-cert-monitor,cost-optimization \
  --connectors postgres,slack,email \
  --profile devops \
  --description "Infrastructure monitoring and SRE operations agent"

docs.title: Configuration Notes
docs.text:
• Define alert routing rules (severity → Slack channel/on-call rotation) in canonical facts
  • Store runbook URLs and escalation policies for incident notifications
  • Configure log sources and their locations for cross-service correlation
  • Set anomaly detection thresholds per service - a 10% CPU spike on a batch worker differs from the API

docs.text:
• Add chaos-engineering for scheduled GameDays
  • Integrate with Terraform or Pulumi state for infrastructure drift detection
  • Add dependency-health to monitor upstream API dependencies
  • Build a capacity-planner forecasting resource needs from growth trends

docs.title: What does the Hermes DevOps Agent do?
docs.text: The Hermes DevOps Agent autonomously monitors infrastructure health every 15 minutes, tracks deployment metrics (DORA), analyzes logs for error patterns, manages incident response with context-rich alerts, and scans for cost optimization opportunities - all delivered to Slack on schedule.

docs.title: How does infrastructure health monitoring work?
docs.text: The agent checks CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics across instances every 15 minutes. When anomalies are detected, it correlates them with recent deployments or traffic changes and alerts with context - not just raw metrics.

docs.title: Can the DevOps agent help during incidents?
docs.text: Yes. During incidents, the agent automatically pulls relevant logs from the window surrounding the alert, identifies recent deployments or config changes, and drafts an incident timeline for post-mortem analysis.

docs.title: What DORA metrics does the agent track?
docs.text: The agent tracks four key DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. Daily reports show trends with week-over-week comparisons.

docs.title: How does the agent handle cost optimization?
docs.text: Every Friday, the agent scans for idle load balancers, oversized instances, unattached volumes, and reserved instance coverage gaps - delivering a prioritized list of savings opportunities.

docs.title: Hermes Sales Agent - Autonomous Pipeline Management & AI Outreach

The Hermes Sales Agent is a production-ready AI sales assistant that automates your entire sales lifecycle - from lead qualification to closed-won deal. Deploy in minutes to monitor your CRM pipeline, enrich lead data, draft outreach sequences, and surface at-risk opportunities so your team spends less time in spreadsheets and more time closing.

This agent runs on the Hermes Agent framework by Nous Research and integrates with your CRM, calendar, and communication tools through CorpusIQ MCP connectors.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Sales Agent replaces manual pipeline management with autonomous monitoring, qualification, and reporting. Instead of checking dashboards and drafting follow-ups manually, your team receives pre-built pipeline summaries, lead scores, and outreach drafts delivered to Slack or email on schedule.

Capability What It Does Pipeline monitoring Daily snapshot of deals by stage, weighted forecast, at-risk flags Lead qualification Scores inbound leads against your ICP using firmographic + behavioral signals Outreach sequencing Drafts multi-touch sequences (email, call, LinkedIn) based on persona and stage Meeting preparation Pulls deal history, contact notes, and recent comms before every call Competitor intelligence Surfaces competitive insights when a competitor appears in a deal record

See also: Agent Library Overview · Marketing Agent · Executive Agent

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Connect your CRM - HubSpot, Close CRM, or LeadConnector via CorpusIQ connectors
  2. Set your ICP - Store ideal customer profile criteria in canonical facts

  4. Schedule the crons - Daily reports, qualification checks, weekly forecasts
  5. Receive in Slack/Email - Pipeline summaries, alerts for stalled deals, meeting briefs

docs.title: Key Features

docs.title: What does the Hermes Support Agent do?
docs.text: The Hermes Support Agent autonomously triages incoming support tickets, searches your knowledge base for answers, drafts response templates, monitors SLA compliance with breach alerts, and detects trending issues from ticket clusters - all on scheduled crons.

docs.title: How does ticket triage work?
docs.text: Every 5 minutes during business hours, the agent scans for unassigned tickets, classifies them by type (billing, technical, account, feature request), checks priority against customer tier, and routes to the appropriate team or queue.

docs.title: Can the agent write responses to customers?
docs.text: Yes. For low-complexity tickets (password resets, billing questions, shipping status), the agent drafts complete responses using knowledge base articles and past resolved tickets. Human agents review and send with one click - the agent never sends without approval.

docs.title: How does SLA monitoring work?
docs.text: The agent checks every 30 minutes for tickets approaching breach. At 50% of SLA, it sends a gentle reminder. At 75%, it notifies the team lead. At 90%, it alerts the manager. After breach, it creates a post-mortem draft.

docs.title: What is trending issue detection?
docs.text: The agent clusters tickets with similar keywords or error messages. When 3+ tickets match within 4 hours, it flags a trending issue on Slack with the common pattern, affected customers, and suggested KB article or escalation path.

docs.title: Production Autonomous Agent Architecture
docs.text:
Most agent implementations follow a common pattern: install the framework, connect an LLM, add tools, and execute tasks through chat. While effective for experimentation, these architectures remain fundamentally human-dependent. The agent can answer questions. The agent cannot operate a business.

A production system requires: long-term memory, persistent identity, workflow orchestration, knowledge consolidation, browser automation, governance controls, authentication management, multi-model optimization, operational monitoring, and autonomous execution.

This document outlines the architecture that bridges that gap.

docs.title: System Architecture - The Six-Layer Model
docs.text: The platform decomposes into six layers, each with distinct responsibilities, failure domains, and scaling characteristics:

docs.title: Layer 1: Agent Orchestration
docs.text:
The brain stem. This layer handles task decomposition, agent routing, model selection, and execution lifecycle management. It receives high-level intent and produces structured workflows.

Components: Hermes Agent (execution kernel), CrewAI (multi-agent coordination), LangGraph (stateful graph execution), Reflexion (self-improvement loops)

Key responsibility: Given a user intent, produce an execution plan and dispatch it to the appropriate agents with the right models.

Data flowing in: Natural language intents, scheduled triggers, event hooks Data flowing out: Structured task graphs, agent assignments, model routing decisions

docs.title: Layer 2: Skills and Tooling
docs.text:
The muscle system. This layer provides domain-specific capabilities - everything the agents can actually do.

Components: 95+ skills across marketing, engineering, operations, and content; 65+ CLI tools; MCP infrastructure with 50+ operational tools; FastMCP validation layer

Key responsibility: Translate agent actions into concrete API calls, database queries, file operations, and external service interactions.

Data flowing in: Structured task definitions from orchestration layer Data flowing out: API responses, file contents, database results, tool outputs

docs.title: Layer 3: Infrastructure
docs.text:
The skeleton. Compute resources, networking, and runtime environments.

Components: Primary compute (DGX-class node for inference and orchestration), worker node (dedicated browser automation and content ops), authentication management, multi-model router, browser automation with Playwright stealth

Key responsibility: Provide reliable, cost-optimized execution environments. Handle model failover, authentication lifecycle, and cross-node communication.

Data flowing in: Execution requests from orchestration, model inference calls Data flowing out: Computation results, browser screenshots, authenticated sessions

docs.title: Layer 4: Content Operations
docs.text:
The voice. Everything the system produces for external consumption.

Components: Video generation pipeline (scripting, avatar rendering, post-production), social publishing engine (multi-platform scheduling, content rotation), engagement system (community response, help-first strategy)

Key responsibility: Generate, schedule, publish, and monitor content across platforms. Handle rate limits, platform-specific formatting, and engagement tracking.

Data flowing in: Content briefs from orchestration, engagement data from platforms Data flowing out: Published posts, videos, comments, engagement reports

docs.title: Layer 5: Knowledge and Memory
docs.text:
The memory. Persistent knowledge that accumulates and compounds over time.

Components: GraphRAG (entity-relationship retrieval), persistent knowledge base (6,000+ indexed pages, vector embeddings, semantic search), dream cycle (nightly consolidation at 03:00), Honcho (conversation memory and peer modeling)

Key responsibility: Store everything learned. Retrieve relevant context instantly. Consolidate knowledge nightly. Never forget.

Data flowing in: Raw conversation data, tool outputs, user interactions, web research Data flowing out: Contextual knowledge for agent decisions, semantic search results, consolidated facts

docs.title: Layer 6: Governance and Operations
docs.text:
The immune system. Monitoring, validation, scheduling, and compliance.

Components: System registry (pre-creation validation), email operations (inbox monitoring for media@ and info@), cron scheduler (140+ scheduled processes), token lifecycle management, model usage tracking

Key responsibility: Ensure everything runs correctly. Detect failures early. Enforce policies. Provide audit trails.

Data flowing in: System metrics, execution logs, token usage, error reports Data flowing out: Alerts, status dashboards, compliance reports, scheduling triggers

docs.title: Data Flow Architecture
docs.text:
graph TD
    U[User Intent] --> O[Orchestration Layer]
    O -->|Task Graph| S[Skills & Tools]
    O -->|Model Route| I[Infrastructure]
    S -->|API Results| O
    I -->|Compute Results| S
    S -->|Published Content| C[Content Ops]
    C -->|Engagement Data| K[Knowledge & Memory]
    S -->|Raw Data| K
    K -->|Context| O
    O -->|Execution Logs| G[Governance]
    G -->|Alerts & Policies| O
    G -->|Scheduled Triggers| O
    K -->|Consolidated Knowledge| K

docs.title: Critical Data Paths
docs.text:
1. Intent-to-Action Path: User Intent → Orchestration decomposes → Skills execute → Results flow back → Knowledge stores. This is the hot path. Latency matters here.

  2. Learning Path: Tool outputs → Knowledge store → Nightly dream cycle → Consolidated facts. This is the compounding path. Throughput matters here, not latency.

  3. Governance Path: Every action → Log → Governance validation → Alert if anomaly. This is the safety path. Completeness matters here.

  4. Content Path: Orchestration generates brief → Content ops produces media → Publishes → Engagement data returns → Knowledge updates strategy. This is the growth path. Consistency matters here.

docs.title: Failure Mode Analysis
docs.text: Every layer has distinct failure modes. Understanding them is critical for designing resilient systems.

docs.title: Layer 1 Failures: Orchestration
docs.text:
Failure Mode Probability Impact Mitigation Model hallucinates execution plan Medium High - wrong task executed Reflexion evaluation loop validates outputs before execution Task decomposition too granular Low Medium - excessive cost Token budget enforcement, plan compression Agent assignment wrong Low High - expensive model for simple task Multi-model router with explicit task-to-model mapping Infinite loop in Reflexion Medium High - cost spiral Max iteration guard (default: 3), cost ceiling per task

Recovery strategy: Orchestration failures are detected by the governance layer monitoring execution anomalies. Recovery involves re-routing to a different model, simplifying the task graph, or escalating to human review.

docs.title: Layer 2 Failures: Skills and Tools
docs.text:
Failure Mode Probability Impact Mitigation API rate limit exceeded High Low - retry fixes it Exponential backoff with jitter, rate limit awareness before calls Tool returns malformed data Medium Medium - downstream corruption Pydantic validation on all tool I/O, schema enforcement External service down Medium Medium - workflow blocked Circuit breaker pattern, degraded-mode execution, cached results Skill version mismatch Low High - silent incorrect behavior Version pinning, checksum validation, canary deployment

Recovery strategy: Tool failures trigger automatic retry with exponential backoff. After three failures, the task is marked for governance review. Critical workflows have fallback tool paths defined.

docs.title: Layer 3 Failures: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Failure Mode Probability Impact Mitigation Model provider rate limit Medium Medium - task backlog Multi-provider routing, queuing with priority, local model fallback Worker node unreachable Low High - browser ops blocked Health checks every 60s, auto-restart via systemd, alert on 3 consecutive failures OAuth token expired High Low - single service blocked Proactive refresh 24h before expiry, automated re-auth flows Disk space exhaustion Low High - system-wide failure 80% threshold alert, automated log rotation, artifact cleanup cron

Recovery strategy: Infrastructure failures use health-check-driven auto-recovery. Persistent failures trigger governance alerts. The system degrades gracefully - if the worker node is down, browser tasks queue until recovery.

docs.title: Layer 4 Failures: Content Operations
docs.text:
Failure Mode Probability Impact Mitigation Platform API changes break publishing Medium Medium - content gap Scheduled integration tests against platform APIs, content queue with retry Video generation fails mid-render Medium Low - wasted compute Render checkpointing, partial output recovery, automated retry Rate limit hit during publish High Low - delayed post Per-platform rate limit tracking, staggered scheduling, backoff Generated content violates platform policy Low High - account risk Pre-publish policy check, content moderation filter, human review flag for edge cases

Recovery strategy: Content ops failures are queued for retry. The system maintains a content buffer (2-3 days of queued content) so transient failures don't create gaps. Policy violations halt the pipeline and require human review.

docs.title: Layer 5 Failures: Knowledge
docs.text:
Failure Mode Probability Impact Mitigation Vector DB corruption Low Critical - knowledge loss Nightly backups, checksum validation, read-repair on retrieval Embedding model drift Low Medium - degraded retrieval A/B test retrieval quality weekly, re-index on score degradation Dream cycle stalls Medium Medium - knowledge fragmentation Timeout guard (max 2 hours), partial commit on timeout, alert on skip Context window overflow Medium Medium - truncated knowledge Token budget management, relevance scoring, hierarchical summarization

Recovery strategy: Knowledge failures are the most dangerous because they compound silently. Nightly validation checks embedding consistency. Weekly retrieval quality benchmarks catch drift. Backups are immutable and versioned.

docs.title: Layer 6 Failures: Governance
docs.text:
Failure Mode Probability Impact Mitigation Alert fatigue (too many false positives) High Medium - real alerts ignored Threshold tuning, alert deduplication, severity tiers Cron job silent failure Medium High - missed execution Outcome validation (not just exit code), heartbeat monitoring Token refresh automation fails Medium Medium - service disruption Multi-channel alerting, manual override path, 48h advance warning Monitoring gap (new component unmonitored) Low High - blind spot Registry-enforced monitoring on creation, automated coverage audit

Recovery strategy: Governance itself must be governed. A meta-monitoring cron validates that all monitoring systems are healthy. Alert pipelines are tested weekly with synthetic failures.

docs.title: Horizontal Scaling
docs.text:
The architecture supports horizontal scaling at several points:

  • Agent instances: Multiple Hermes instances can process tasks in parallel, coordinated through a shared task queue
  • Worker nodes: Additional Mac Mini or equivalent nodes can be provisioned for browser automation, content rendering, or other CPU-intensive tasks
  • Model providers: The multi-model router can distribute inference across providers, avoiding single-provider bottlenecks

docs.title: Vertical Scaling
docs.text:
• Primary compute: Upgrading the inference node improves all LLM-dependent operations
  • Memory allocation: Larger context windows enable more complex reasoning chains
  • Storage: Expanding the knowledge base requires proportional storage growth (approximately 1GB per 1,000 indexed documents)

docs.title: Cost Optimization
docs.text:
The multi-model router achieves approximately 65% cost reduction versus premium-model-only routing by matching task complexity to model capability:

  • Tier 1 (Lightweight): Local models for classification, formatting, simple extraction - near-zero cost
  • Tier 2 (Standard): Mid-tier cloud models for content generation, tool selection, analysis
  • Tier 3 (Premium): Top-tier models for strategic reasoning, multi-step planning, critical decisions

docs.title: Decision Tree for Architecture Choices
docs.text:
When building your own deployment, use this decision framework:

  1. Do you need multi-agent coordination?
  2. Yes, complex workflows with specialization → Add CrewAI

  3. No, linear task execution is sufficient → Hermes alone

  4. Do you need persistent memory across sessions?

  5. Yes, cumulative knowledge matters → Full knowledge layer (GraphRAG + dream cycle)

  6. No, each session is independent → Stateless execution

  7. Do you need browser automation?

  8. Yes, for web research, social media, form filling → Dedicated worker node

  9. No → Skip worker infrastructure

  10. Do you need content generation at scale?

  11. Yes, multiple platforms, daily cadence → Full content ops layer

  12. No, occasional posts → Manual or simplified pipeline

  13. What's your availability requirement?

  14. 24/7 autonomous operation → All six layers, full governance
  15. Business hours, human-in-the-loop → Layers 1-3, simplified governance

  16. Experimentation only → Layer 1 only

  17. What's your budget model?

  18. Cost-optimized → Multi-model routing, local models for simple tasks
  19. Performance-first → Premium models only, dedicated compute
  20. Balanced → Tiered routing with cost ceilings

docs.title: Integration Points
docs.text:
The architecture layers communicate through well-defined interfaces:

  • Orchestration ↔ Skills: Task graph format (JSON with typed actions)
  • Skills ↔ Infrastructure: Tool execution protocol (standardized I/O with Pydantic schemas)
  • Infrastructure ↔ Content: Content job format (platform, media type, schedule, metadata)
  • Content ↔ Knowledge: Engagement event format (platform, metric, timestamp, context)
  • All layers → Governance: Structured log format (layer, component, action, status, metadata)

Each interface is versioned. Breaking changes require a migration period where both old and new formats are accepted.

docs.title: Security Boundaries
docs.text:
• Network: Worker node on isolated VLAN, accessible only from primary compute
  • Authentication: OAuth tokens stored encrypted at rest, rotated proactively
  • Data: Knowledge base encrypted, access logged, retention policies enforced
  • Execution: Skills run in sandboxed environments, tool calls validated before dispatch

docs.title: The AI Consistency Problem No One Is Talking About
docs.text:
Every business owner who has used AI tools has hit this. You ask ChatGPT for this month's revenue. It gives you a number. Then you ask Claude the same question. Different number. Perplexity. A third number.

Same business. Same data. Same question. Three different answers.

This is not a hallucination problem. It is a data access problem.

docs.title: Where the Numbers Come From
docs.text:
When you ask an AI about your business, it has three options for answering:

Option 1: Training data. The AI guesses based on patterns it learned during training. It might say "$50,000" because that is a common small business revenue number, not because it looked at your actual data. This is the AI equivalent of a stranger guessing your salary.

Option 2: Web search. The AI searches the open web. If your revenue is public anywhere (investor decks, press releases, blog posts), it might find it. If it is not public, the AI is searching for something that does not exist.

Option 3: Direct access. The AI connects to your actual business tools. Shopify for orders. Stripe for payments. QuickBooks for books. GA4 for traffic. Every answer traces back to live data. Same sources. Same answer. Every AI. Every time.

docs.title: Why Option 3 Is the Only One That Matters
docs.text:
Training data gives you numbers from six months ago. Web search gives you numbers you intentionally made public. Direct access gives you the numbers your business actually runs on.

The consistency problem disappears when every AI pulls from the same source. Not because the AI got smarter. Because the data pipeline replaced guessing with verification.

docs.title: What This Requires
docs.text:
Most business tools were not designed for AI access. They were designed for humans to log in and look at dashboards. Connecting them to AI requires:

  • Read-only OAuth so the AI can see data but never modify it
  • Per-source authentication so each tool validates independently
  • Metric definitions so revenue means the same thing across every system
  • Source citations so every answer traces back to the original data
  • Cross-AI compatibility so ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity all get the same numbers

This is infrastructure work. It is not flashy. No one tweets about OAuth scopes. But it is the difference between an AI that guesses about your business and an AI that knows your business.

docs.title: The Bottom Line
docs.text:
Ask your AI a question about your business right now. Write down the answer. Now ask a different AI the same question. If the numbers do not match, you do not have an AI problem. You have a data access problem.

The fix is not a better model. It is a better pipe.

docs.title: How Business AI Agents Handle Data Access - The Infrastructure Layer
docs.text: Every business owner who has tried asking ChatGPT about their revenue has hit the same wall. The AI is capable. The data is there. But there is no pipe between them.

docs.title: The Three-Layer Stack
docs.text: Business AI data access needs three layers:

docs.title: Layer 1: Connectors
docs.text:
Raw API integrations. OAuth to Shopify. API key to Stripe. Service account to GA4. Each connector handles authentication, rate limiting, error retry, and data normalization independently. No shared session. No cross-contamination.

This is where most platforms stop. They give you connectors and call it done. But connectors alone do not answer business questions. They return raw data.

docs.title: Layer 2: Resolution
docs.text:
When a user asks "what was revenue last month," the system must resolve that question across multiple connectors. Shopify has orders. Stripe has payments. QuickBooks has invoices. Each defines revenue differently. Each has different date boundaries.

Resolution means: - Mapping the business question to connector-specific queries - Normalizing date ranges across timezone-aware systems - Resolving entity conflicts (is this Shopify customer the same as this QuickBooks customer?) - Merging results without double-counting

This layer is what makes "one answer" possible across multiple sources.

docs.title: Layer 3: Validation
docs.text:
Every answer must trace back to its source. "Revenue was $142,000 last month" is useless without "Shopify: $89,000 (1,247 orders), Stripe: $38,000 (subscriptions), QuickBooks: $15,000 (consulting invoices)."

Validation means: - Source citations on every number - Conflict detection (Shopify says $89K, Stripe says $86K for the same period) - Audit trail from answer back to raw API response

docs.title: Why Stateless Matters
docs.text:
The stateless MCP specification (protocol version 2026-07-28) makes this architecture practical at scale. Every connector call is a discrete HTTP request with its own authentication. No sessions. No connection state. No sticky routing.

docs.title: The Harness Beats the Model - Why AI Infrastructure Matters More Than AI Models
docs.text: The biggest insight in AI right now is not about models. It is about harnesses.

docs.title: What a Harness Is
docs.text:
A harness is the runtime wrapper around an AI model. The code that gives it tools. Feeds it context. Executes its tool calls. Decides when the run is finished. Handles errors. Manages memory. The harness is everything around the model that makes the model useful.

Most AI products compete on models. GPT vs Claude. Opus vs Sonnet. The model wars get all the attention.

But here is what the research shows: the harness matters more.

docs.title: The Evidence
docs.text:
HuggingFace published "Don't Train the Model, Evolve the Harness" in July 2026. They took a frozen open model (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) that scored 0% on Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark. They rewrote only the harness. The scaffold. The code around the model.

The result: whole-task success went from 0% to 5.0% and criterion pass rate from 63.4% to 80.1% on a held-out test set the loop never saw. The frozen open model landed between Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 on the headline metric. Zero model weights changed.

This is called the mismanaged geniuses hypothesis: capable models held back by brittle, hand-built scaffolds. A weak score often measures the harness, not the model.

The Meta-Harness loop (Lee et al., 2026) automated this process. A Claude proposer (Opus 4.8) reads run history, copies the current best harness, adds one mechanism, and an outer loop keeps it only if it clears a noise margin on a 24-task dev set. The harness self-improves while the model stays frozen.

Another study found that Claude Opus 4.5 went from 52.1% to 57.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 just by changing the harness. Same model. Different scaffold. A 65x gap in input tokens between the two runs (256.9M versus 3.9M).

AWS engineers took Claude Opus 5 from 30% on ARC-AGI-3 to 99.95% by wrapping it in an open-source agent harness, the Strands SDK. The model did not change. The code around it did.
