docs.title: Read-Only External-Source Retrieval: Why AI Should Never Write to Your Business Tools
docs.text:
Every business tool you use contains data that should never be modified by AI. Your QuickBooks general ledger. Your Shopify orders. Your Stripe transactions. Your HubSpot CRM records.

Connecting AI to these tools requires a hard boundary: read everything, write nothing.

docs.title: The Risk of AI Write Access
docs.text:
AI models are probabilistic. They are right most of the time but wrong some of the time. When an AI writes an email draft, a mistake means an awkward sentence. When an AI modifies your QuickBooks, a mistake means corrupted financials.

Write access risks include:

Financial errors: A miscategorized transaction. A payment applied to the wrong invoice. An expense recorded in the wrong period. Each error compounds through your books.

Data corruption: Overwriting valid records. Creating duplicate entries. Deleting historical data that seemed irrelevant to the AI but was needed for audit.

Compliance violations: Modifying records in ways that break audit trails. Changing transactions after close periods. Altering data subject to regulatory retention requirements.

Security exposure: Write access is a broader attack surface. If an AI with write access is compromised, every tool it can write to is compromised.

docs.title: How Read-Only External-Source Retrieval Works
docs.text:
Read-only OAuth gives AI permission to query data but blocks all write operations. The authorization flow is:

  1. You log into your tool (Shopify, QuickBooks, Stripe, etc.)
  2. You grant read-only access to the AI connector
  3. The connector receives a token scoped to read-only operations
  4. Every API call uses this token - the tool's own security rejects any write attempt

Even if the AI tries to modify data, the tool itself blocks the operation. The boundary is enforced at the API level, not the AI level.

One distinction worth stating plainly: external retrieval is read-only, but some platforms also expose configuration or control-plane operations outside the retrieval path. Those operations change scoped platform state, so they are named and annotated separately instead of being folded into the read-only claim. Ask any provider to draw that line explicitly.

docs.title: Per-Source Authentication
docs.text:
Each tool gets its own read-only external-source retrieval token. Shopify has one token. QuickBooks has another. Stripe has a third. No shared credentials. No master key.

This means: - Compromising one connector does not compromise others - Revoking access to one tool does not affect others - Each tool maintains its own audit log of AI queries - You can see exactly what data each AI accessed and when

docs.title: What Read-Only Means in Practice
docs.text:
Shopify: Query orders, products, customers, and analytics. Cannot create orders, modify inventory, or process refunds.

QuickBooks: Query chart of accounts, transactions, reports, and vendor data. Cannot create invoices, modify journal entries, or reconcile accounts.

Stripe: Query payments, subscriptions, customers, and disputes. Cannot process charges, issue refunds, or modify subscriptions.

HubSpot: Query contacts, deals, companies, and tickets. Cannot create records, modify pipelines, or send emails.

GA4: Query traffic, conversions, and audience data. Cannot modify tracking settings or data streams.

docs.title: Why This Matters for AI Business Intelligence
docs.text:
The promise of AI business intelligence is that you can ask any question about your business and get a verified answer. That promise only works if the AI can access your data without putting it at risk.

Read-only access means: - Verified answers from live data - Retrieval operations do not modify their source records - Complete audit trail of every query - Per-source security boundaries

This is not a feature. It is the foundation of trust between AI and business data.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
When evaluating AI data access platforms, inspect provider scopes and tool-level safety metadata separately. Confirm that retrieval operations are marked read-only, identify any write-capable management or control-plane operations, ask what the platform retains, and check whether access is auditable.

If a platform cannot answer these questions clearly, it does not have the security boundary your business data requires.

The difference between read-only and read-write is the difference between safe intelligence and unnecessary risk.

docs.title: The Source of Truth Problem - Why Every Business Dashboard Lies
docs.text:
Every business runs on numbers. Revenue. Margin. Churn. CAC. LTV. These numbers determine budgets, hiring, strategy, and survival.

Here is the problem: none of your tools agree on what these numbers mean.

docs.title: The Same Metric, Four Different Answers
docs.text:
Ask four different tools for your monthly revenue:

Shopify counts gross merchandise value. Every order at full price. Discounts applied later. Refunds processed separately.

Stripe counts processed payments. Net of fees. Net of refunds. Different settlement timing than order date.

QuickBooks counts invoiced revenue. Based on accounting rules. Accrual or cash basis. Different recognition dates than transaction dates.

GA4 counts attributed revenue. Only from tracked channels. Attribution windows vary. Cross-device de-duplication changes numbers.

Four tools. Four different definitions of revenue. All of them are correct. None of them agree.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
When your team sits down on Monday morning to review the numbers, someone is always wrong. Not because they made a mistake. Because they pulled from a different source.

The Shopify person says $142,000. The QuickBooks person says $138,000. The Stripe person says $135,000. The argument is not about accuracy. It is about definitions. And nobody wrote down what revenue actually means.

docs.title: The Fix: Declared Source of Truth
docs.text:
Before you can automate anything, you must define what you are measuring. Not in a dashboard tool. Not in a spreadsheet. In a declaration that every system references.

For revenue, the declaration might be: "Gross order value from Shopify at the time of order placement, excluding tax and shipping, for orders with status not equal to cancelled or fully refunded."

Every system can then be evaluated against this definition. The numbers still will not match perfectly. But now you know why they differ. And you know which number is the official one.

docs.title: Beyond Revenue
docs.text:
This problem affects every metric:

  • Customer count: Shopify counts customers by email. Stripe by payment method. HubSpot by contact record. Three different counts of the same people.
  • Churn: Subscription cancellation vs. payment failure vs. no-login-in-90-days. Three different definitions, three different churn rates.
  • Margin: Revenue minus cost of goods. But which revenue definition? Which cost inclusion rules? Direct costs only or allocated overhead?

docs.title: What This Means for AI
docs.text:
When you connect AI to your business tools, the definition problem becomes critical. The AI will pull from multiple sources. If revenue is not defined, the AI will reconcile the numbers however it sees fit. You will get an answer. You will not know if it is right.

The solution is to define each metric once, store those definitions as canonical facts, and have every AI query reference them. The AI does not decide what revenue means. You do. The AI just does the math.

docs.title: The Bottom Line
docs.text:
Your dashboard is not lying to you. It is just answering a different question than you think you asked. Define the question first. Then build the dashboard. Or better yet, let AI answer questions against your definitions, not against the default ones each vendor ships.

Consistent answers require consistent definitions. Everything else is just four different numbers on one screen.

docs.title: Stateless MCP - What the July 2026 Spec Means for Business AI
docs.text:
The MCP specification update on July 28, 2026 retired the initialize/initialized handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header that used to follow it. MCP now has a stateless protocol core - every request carries its own protocol version, client identity, and capabilities, so a tool call needs no prior session context.

This matters for business operators because it removes the single biggest barrier to connecting real business data to AI: infrastructure complexity.

docs.title: The Old Way (Pre-July 2026)
docs.text:
Under the 2025-11-25 revision, Streamable HTTP carried a protocol-level session: the server minted a session ID in the Mcp-Session-Id header, the client could open a standalone SSE stream with an HTTP GET, servers could send JSON-RPC requests on that stream, and streams were resumable with Last-Event-ID. A dropped connection cost you the session. That meant:

  • A session belonged to one server instance, so replicas needed a shared session store or sticky routing
  • Load balancing was difficult (sticky sessions required)
  • Scaling meant managing session stores and open streams
  • Every new connector added connection overhead

docs.title: The New Way (Post-July 2026)
docs.text:
A single HTTP POST carries everything. No handshake. No session ID. No persistent connection.

POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: search
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call",
 "params":{"name":"search","arguments":{"q":"current revenue"},
 "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28",
          "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo":{"name":"my-app","version":"1.0"},
          "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}

The body is the source of truth: the protocol version and client capabilities travel in _meta on every request. Streamable HTTP additionally mirrors selected fields into the three headers above (MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method, Mcp-Name) so proxies can route without parsing the body, and a server rejects a request whose header and body disagree.

Servers must implement server/discover, which advertises supported protocol versions, capabilities, and identity. Clients may call it first for up-front version selection instead of handshaking.

This is the same pattern REST APIs have used for decades. Any HTTP server can serve MCP. Any load balancer can distribute requests. Any CDN can cache where appropriate.

docs.title: Why This Matters for Business Data
docs.text:
Stateless MCP means business data connectors can be:

Read-only and request-scoped. Each request authenticates independently. Direct MCP does not retain raw customer files or full connector response payloads. Operational query metadata and bounded outcome summaries may be retained for up to 30 days.

Per-user scoped. Each user's OAuth token travels with the request. Shopify and QuickBooks remain the authoritative systems. Raw customer files and full connector response payloads are not aggregated into a CorpusIQ warehouse; scoped operational retention still applies.

Infrastructure-independent. No WebSocket servers to maintain. No session state to manage. Standard HTTP infrastructure works - Cloudflare, AWS ALB, nginx.

Cross-AI compatible. The same connector serves ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and any other MCP-compatible AI. The user chooses their AI. The data layer stays consistent.

docs.title: What CorpusIQ Adds
docs.text:
Stateless MCP solves the transport problem. But business operators need more than transport:

  • 40+ pre-built connectors for Shopify, QuickBooks, Stripe, GA4, Meta Ads, HubSpot, and more
  • Metric definitions that ensure revenue means the same thing across every AI and every connector
  • Source-of-truth validation that traces every answer back to the original system
  • Read-only OAuth so no AI can modify your business data
  • Scoped retention - connectors fetch live data without retaining raw customer files or full response payloads; operational logs may persist for up to 30 days

The stateless MCP spec makes this architecture possible at scale. No connection pools. No session affinity. No state to lose.

docs.title: The Industry Shift
docs.text:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway added 2026-07-28 to the protocol versions it serves, opt-in per gateway. Google published scaling guidance. Simon Willison wrote that stateless MCP has "recaptured my interest" and built three MCP tools off the new spec.

The direction is clear: AI data access is moving toward stateless, authenticated, per-request patterns. The same architecture that made REST APIs the backbone of the web is now coming to AI tool access.

For business operators, this means your QuickBooks, Shopify, and Stripe data can reach any AI you use - without building infrastructure, managing connections, or storing data in intermediate systems.

docs.text:

docs.title: The Real Fix

Connect your business tools directly to AI. Not through dashboards. Not through CSV exports. Direct, read-only, authenticated access.

When ChatGPT asks "what was revenue last month," the system queries Shopify, Stripe, and QuickBooks simultaneously. Returns one number. Cites every source. Same answer in Claude. Same answer in Perplexity.

This is not a better AI model. It is a better data pipeline.

The answer: "$142,000 - Shopify: $89,000 (1,247 orders), Stripe: $38,000 (subscriptions), QuickBooks: $15,000 (consulting invoices). Sources: Shopify Orders API, Stripe Payments API, QuickBooks Profit & Loss."

Same question in Claude. Same answer. Same question in Perplexity. Same answer.

The AI did not get smarter. The data pipeline eliminated the guesswork.

Most businesses run on 20 to 40 tools. Shopify for sales. Stripe for payments. QuickBooks for accounting. GA4 for analytics. Meta Ads for marketing. HubSpot for CRM. Klaviyo for email.

Each one holds part of the answer. No one tool has the full picture. The AI needs to see across all of them simultaneously, in real time, with read-only access.

This is the infrastructure layer that turns AI from a writing assistant into a business operating system.

docs.title: Hermes Agent Best Practices - Build Reliable AI Automation
docs.text: Hermes Agent best practices capture what the community has learned about building reliable, secure, and maintainable AI agent setups. Whether you're running your first cron or managing a team deployment, these best practices help you avoid the mistakes we've already made in production.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This guide serves as the entry point to the Hermes Agent best practices collection. Each companion guide (cron design, model selection, memory management, security, skill development, MCP design) stands alone - read the ones relevant to your current work.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The best practices follow four core principles that apply across every aspect of Hermes Agent operation:

Explicit over implicit. Hermes Agent should do what you told it to do, not what it guessed you meant. Explicit tools, explicit permissions, explicit confirmations. The best Hermes setup is the one where you never wonder "why did it do that?"

Observable over magical. Every automated decision should be traceable. Every cron should log its work. Every skill invocation should leave an audit trail. Debugging a Hermes pipeline should be a matter of reading logs, not guessing.

Composable over monolithic. Small, focused skills compose into powerful workflows. A single "do everything" skill is brittle. Five well-scoped skills that chain together are flexible and testable.

Least privilege by default. Start with read-only access. Add write capabilities only when the use case demands it. Add approval gates before write capabilities go live.

docs.title: Anti-Patterns Quick Reference
docs.text:
These patterns cause the majority of production incidents. Avoid them.

docs.title: What is the most important Hermes Agent best practice?
docs.text: Start with least-privilege access (read-only) and add write capabilities only when needed with explicit approval gates. This single practice prevents the majority of production incidents.

docs.title: How do I know if my Hermes Agent setup is production-ready?

docs.title: Should I use local or cloud models for production?

docs.title: How do I prevent cron jobs from causing problems?
docs.text: Follow cron design best practices: make every cron idempotent, implement retry with backoff, alert on persistent failure, and never run unbounded queries.

docs.title: 12-Factor Agents - Production Engineering Standards for AI Agents
docs.text:
Most agent demos are a prompt, a bag of tools, and a loop that runs until the goal is reached. Most agent failures in production happen because exactly that pattern was shipped. The 12-Factor Agents framework by Dex and the HumanLayer team, in the spirit of Heroku's 12-Factor App, replaces the demo loop with twelve concrete engineering principles. The core argument: production-grade agents are mostly deterministic software, with LLM steps placed at exactly the right points - not end-to-end LLM reasoning.

This guide maps each of the twelve factors onto Hermes Agent, showing what "mostly deterministic software" looks like on a real production agent stack, which factors are already native to the architecture, and where the honest gaps remain.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The twelve factors below read like a checklist for turning a fragile agent prototype into reliable infrastructure. Each factor answers a specific failure mode:

Factor Failure Mode It Fixes 1. Natural language to tool calls Models improvising actions instead of calling typed tools 2. Own your prompts Prompts living in vendor UIs, unreviewed and unversioned 3. Own your context window Context assembled by accident, stuffed until it breaks 4. Tools as structured outputs Tools returning prose that downstream steps cannot parse 5. Unify execution and business state The agent's state and the business's state drifting apart 6. Launch/pause/resume with simple APIs Jobs that cannot be stopped or resumed cleanly 7. Contact humans with tool calls Escalation as an afterthought instead of a tool 8. Own your control flow Hidden framework loops the operator cannot inspect 9. Compact errors into context Blind retries and silent failures 10. Small focused agents God-agents that fail everywhere at once 11. Trigger from anywhere Agents that can only run inside a chat window 12. Stateless reducer State that exists only in memory, lost on restart

docs.title: 1. Natural Language to Tool Calls
docs.text:
The principle: The model's job is to decide which tool to call, not to improvise the action itself. Tools are typed functions with schemas; the runtime executes them deterministically.

How Hermes implements it: Every capability - email, search, files, social publishing, monitoring - is a schema-validated tool. A model output that says "I will send an email" without a tool call does nothing. The execution path is code, the decision step is the LLM, and the two never blur.

docs.title: 2. Own Your Prompts
docs.text:
The principle: Prompts are code. They live in version control, they are reviewed, and they change deliberately - not inside a vendor's settings page.

How Hermes implements it: The system prompt, operating constitution, and procedural skills are all versioned files in the agent's profile directory. Changing behavior means changing a file with an audit trail, exactly like changing application code. Prompt drift is a code review problem, not a mystery.

docs.title: 3. Own Your Context Window
docs.text:
The principle: You decide what enters context for each task. Context is assembled deliberately from the right memory tiers, not accumulated as the conversation scrolls.

How Hermes implements it: A layered memory stack serves context on demand: a small hot-facts file for per-turn essentials, semantic peer memory for identity and preferences, an organizational knowledge graph for project relationships, and durable disk for raw archives. Each layer is queried for what the current task needs. This factor is also the product thesis behind CorpusIQ itself: businesses deserve the same discipline - cited answers pulled from their own sources, in the context window of the AI they already use, instead of an ungoverned prompt loop.

docs.title: 4. Tools as Structured Outputs
docs.text:
The principle: Tools return structured data - JSON with schemas - not prose. Downstream steps consume, validate, and log that data without parsing natural language.

How Hermes implements it: Tool results carry typed fields that downstream logic branches on. A social post returns a post ID and status; a lead query returns a structured record. Composing tools means composing schemas, which keeps multi-step workflows parseable end to end.

docs.title: 5. Unify Execution and Business State
docs.text:
The principle: The agent's execution state and the business's state are the same record. There is one ledger, and both sides read it.

How Hermes implements it: Append-only event logs are the single source of truth for what ran, what was posted, what was sent, and which leads are where in the pipeline. The agent's "did I do this" question and the operator's "what happened this week" question are answered from the same files. State is a log, not a variable.

docs.title: 6. Launch/Pause/Resume with Simple APIs
docs.text:
The principle: Every job can be launched, paused, resumed, and listed from the command line. Long-running work survives restarts and operator intervention.

How Hermes implements it: The scheduler exposes plain CLI operations for every scheduled job, and durable task records persist work-in-progress across crashes and restarts. A job is never a black box that must run to completion or die trying.

docs.title: 7. Contact Humans with Tool Calls
docs.text:
The principle: Escalating to a human is a tool call like any other - logged, traceable, and triggered by policy - not a side effect the agent happens to perform.

How Hermes implements it: Alerts, approval gates, and handoffs are first-class tools. When a workflow needs a human decision, it calls the escalation tool with structured context, and that call lands in the same audit trail as every other action.

docs.title: 8. Own Your Control Flow
docs.text:
The principle: No hidden framework loop. The operator can read the sequence of steps, the gates, and the fallbacks, because they are explicit and versioned.

How Hermes implements it: Workflows are explicit step sequences with pre-flight gates, kill switches, and fallback chains defined in files. If something goes wrong, the failure mode was written down before it happened, and the operator can point at the exact step.

docs.title: 9. Compact Errors into Context
docs.text:
The principle: When a step fails, the error is summarized and injected into context so the next attempt is informed - not a blind retry, not a silent crash.

How Hermes implements it: Partially. Error reporting is structured and persistent, and recovery paths are explicit. Formal error compaction - automatically distilling failure context into the next attempt's context window - is the top gap on this list. Most failures are handled by policy gates rather than by learned correction.

docs.title: 10. Small Focused Agents
docs.text:
The principle: One agent, one responsibility. Small agents fail small, are easy to review, and compose into larger systems.

How Hermes implements it: Procedural skills are single-responsibility by design, and production work is split into focused agent families - one for email operations, one for social publishing, one for system health. Each family owns a narrow surface and a shared ledger. A god-agent that does everything is an anti-pattern documented in the best practices overview.

docs.title: 11. Trigger from Anywhere
docs.text:
The principle: The same workflow can start from a schedule, a webhook, an inbox signal, or an API client. Triggers are external events; agents do not self-loop forever.

How Hermes implements it: Workflows are entry-point agnostic. The email operation that runs on a schedule is the same logic an MCP client can invoke directly. Triggering is decoupled from execution, so the agent never needs to run continuously to be alive.

docs.title: 12. Stateless Reducer
docs.text:
The principle: State is derived by reducing an event log. Given the events, any state can be reconstructed - so nothing critical lives only in memory.

How Hermes implements it: Partially. The operational state is event-sourced in append-only logs, which makes most state reconstructable. Formal reducer semantics - a single pure function that folds events into state, applied uniformly - is the second gap. The discipline of "state is a log" is in place; the formalism is not yet complete.

docs.title: The Two Honest Gaps
docs.text:
Scoring the stack against all twelve factors, two are partially implemented:

  1. Factor 9 - Compact errors into context. Failures are logged and gated, but error context is not yet automatically distilled into the next attempt. This is the highest-leverage reliability improvement available.
  2. Factor 12 - Stateless reducer. Event sourcing is the default for operational state, but a uniform reducer formalism across all workflows would make replay and recovery fully mechanical.

Both gaps are engineering work items, not architecture flaws - the current design supports them without rework.

docs.title: Adoption Checklist
docs.text:
Adopting 12-factor discipline for your own agent stack, in order of impact:

  1. Version your prompts like code. System prompts and skills in git, changes reviewed.
  2. Define tool schemas before agent logic. Every capability gets a typed contract first.
  3. Log every external action to an append-only ledger. State is a log.
  4. Wire escalation as a tool call. Alerts and approvals flow through the audit trail.
  5. Give every job pause/resume semantics. No black-box runs.
  6. Summarize errors into context. Replace blind retries with informed retries.
  7. Split god-agents into focused skills. Small agents fail small.
  8. Make workflows trigger-agnostic. Schedule, webhook, inbox, and API should be interchangeable entry points.
  9. Derive state from events. Where you can replay, you can recover.

docs.title: What are the 12-Factor Agents?
docs.text: A production engineering framework for AI agents, in the spirit of Heroku's 12-Factor App, created by Dex and the HumanLayer team. It replaces the "prompt plus tools plus loop" prototype with twelve concrete principles for deterministic, operable, reliable agent software. Full source: github.com/humanlayer/12-factor-agents.

docs.title: Which factor matters most for reliability?
docs.text: Factors 1 through 4 - natural language to tool calls, own your prompts, own your context window, and tools as structured outputs. They convert an agent from a language model wrapped in a loop into software with typed contracts, versioned configuration, and deliberate context assembly. Everything after factor 4 builds on that foundation.

docs.title: Does Hermes Agent implement all twelve factors?
docs.text: Ten of the twelve are native to the Hermes architecture and implemented in production. Two are partial: factor 9 (compact errors into context) and factor 12 (stateless reducer). Both are engineering work items on the existing architecture, not redesigns.

docs.title: How do I adopt the 12 factors in my own agent stack?
docs.text: Start with the adoption checklist above: version your prompts, define tool schemas first, log every external action to an append-only ledger, and wire escalation as a tool call. Those four moves eliminate the majority of production agent incidents regardless of which framework you run.

docs.title: Agent Capability Audit - the "4 must-install plugins" test
docs.text: A popular Hermes-ecosystem creator published a checklist video: "Do not run Hermes Agent another week without installing these 4 plugins first." The video names no products - it names four capabilities. We transcribed the video and audited the CorpusIQ stack against each one.

docs.title: The 4 capabilities (from the video)
docs.text:
1. Live cost control - monitors what the agent actually spends on model usage while it runs, so you find out before the bill arrives.
  2. Model picker - switch models on the fly instead of being locked into the setup-time configuration: cheap models for grunt work, expensive ones when the task demands it.
  3. Goal management - the agent holds objectives across sessions instead of thinking one conversation at a time.
  4. Agent bridge - lets your agent hand work to your other agents instead of you copying context around manually. The same suite includes WhatsApp and Discord voice bridges.

docs.title: CorpusIQ stack mapping
docs.text: Capability What we run Verdict Live cost control Token-usage monitoring on every session plus cost attribution tracking across the fleet Covered Model picker A model router with a cost ladder (cheap primary, escalation tiers for complex work) Covered Goal management Semantic memory + session handoff + knowledge-graph notes so objectives persist across sessions Covered Agent bridge MCP server for tool sharing across agents + email delivery for human-facing reports Partial - no WhatsApp voice bridge (Hermes covers Discord voice channels natively)

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: The checklist is satisfied by Hermes-native capabilities (cost tracking, model routing, persistent memory, MCP) - no third-party plugin is required to cover the four categories. The one genuine gap versus the creator's suite is the WhatsApp voice bridge: Hermes voice mode covers the CLI and live conversations in Discord voice channels natively, so Discord is not a gap. The CorpusIQ fleet delivers its agent-to-human output by email. If agent reach on WhatsApp becomes a priority, that bridge is the addition to make.

docs.title: Lighthouse Agentic Browsing: The AI-Readiness Audit Standard
docs.text:
Google added an Agentic Browsing category to Lighthouse in 13.3 (7 May 2026), shipped in the DevTools of Chrome 150 and enabled in the default config from that release. The current Lighthouse release is 13.6 (27 October 2026). Instead of measuring how a page performs for human visitors, it measures how ready a page is for AI agents and agentic browsers: can an agent find a machine-readable summary of the site, call its tools, parse its structure, and render it without layout fighting?

The category is experimental and based on proposed standards. It requires Chrome 150 or later, and the WebMCP audits require registering for the WebMCP origin trial.

For anyone working on GEO (generative engine optimization) and AEO (answer engine optimization), this is the first standardized, checkable target. You can audit a site in one command and track the score the same way teams track Core Web Vitals.

docs.title: The four signals
docs.text:
Signal What it checks Score impact llms.txt A machine-readable site summary at /llms.txt Presence, structure, and links WebMCP Declared browser tools (navigator.modelContext.registerTool()) plus a manifest Declaration via script, link, or meta tag Accessibility tree lang, landmarks, labels, and alt text coverage Integrity of the tree agents parse Layout stability Media with intrinsic dimensions or reserved space No shifting elements during agent render

An agent that cannot parse your accessibility tree or that sees your layout jump mid-render has the same experience a human has on a broken mobile page. These four signals are the machine-readable equivalent of usability.

docs.title: How to audit
docs.text:
Run Lighthouse with the agentic browsing category enabled:

npx lighthouse https://example.com --view --only-categories=agentic-browsing

This category is not scored like Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices or SEO. Lighthouse reports a fractional pass ratio (how many of the agentic readiness checks pass), a pass/fail status per audit, and informational counts in the category header. There is no weighted 0 to 100 score and no letter grade, because the standards for the agentic web are still emerging. Track the pass ratio as the number to move. You can also score a single page with any tool that implements the same four checks, which is useful in CI to fail a build that regresses.

docs.title: 1. llms.txt
docs.text:
Publish a plain-text summary at your site root. Keep it short, structured, and linked:

# Example Product

> One line on what the product does and who it is for.

## Docs
- [Quickstart](https://example.com/docs/quickstart): install and first run
- [API reference](https://example.com/docs/api): endpoints and auth

## Optional
- [Pricing](https://example.com/pricing)

docs.title: 2. WebMCP
docs.text:
Expose the actions agents may take, directly from the page:

<script>
navigator.modelContext?.registerTool({
  name: "search_docs",
  description: "Search the documentation",
  inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string" } } },
  execute: async ({ query }) => search(query)
});
</script>

Declare the manifest with a text/mcp script or meta tag so scanners can find it without executing the page.

docs.title: 3. Accessibility tree
docs.text:
• Set lang on the root element.
  • Use landmarks: header, nav, main, footer.
  • Give every image alt text; decorative images get an empty alt="".
  • Label every form control.

docs.title: 4. Layout stability
docs.text: Add explicit width and height attributes to img, iframe, and video elements, or reserve space in CSS with aspect-ratio. This is the same fix that improves Core Web Vitals CLS, measured for agents instead of humans.

docs.title: Checklist before you ship
docs.text:
• [ ] /llms.txt exists and is well formed
  • [ ] WebMCP tools are declared and reachable
  • [ ] lang, landmarks, alt text, and labels are complete
  • [ ] All media declare intrinsic dimensions
  • [ ] Lighthouse agentic browsing score recorded on the release checklist

docs.title: What is Lighthouse Agentic Browsing?
docs.text: It is a Lighthouse category added in May 2026 that scores how ready a page is for AI agents and agentic browsers. It checks four signals: llms.txt presence, WebMCP integration, accessibility-tree integrity, and layout stability.

docs.title: Is this the same as SEO?
docs.text: It overlaps with technical SEO, but it targets machine consumers instead of search crawlers. A page can rank well and still score poorly here if it lacks llms.txt, declared tools, or stable layout.

docs.title: How often should I run the audit?
docs.text: Run it on every deploy in CI, and review the full site monthly. Score regressions usually come from new pages that ship without llms.txt updates or media without dimensions.

docs.title: Cron Design Best Practices - Reliable Scheduled Automation
docs.text: Scheduled automation is one of Hermes Agent's most powerful features, but poorly designed crons are the fastest path to operational pain. These cron design best practices cover idempotency, error handling, rate limiting, monitoring, and the anti-patterns that keep your scheduled tasks reliable and safe in production.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Crons are the heartbeat of autonomous Hermes Agent operation. They handle email monitoring, data synchronization, report generation, and operational checks - running on schedules from every 5 minutes to once per month. Following Hermes Agent best practices for cron design prevents silent failures, resource exhaustion, and alert fatigue.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A well-designed Hermes Agent cron follows this pattern:

SCHEDULE → DATA COLLECTION → PROCESSING → VALIDATION → OUTPUT → LOGGING
                                                         ↓
                                                    ERROR → RETRY → DEAD-LETTER → ALERT

docs.title: What Hermes cron actually gives you
docs.text:
Verified against the official cron documentation and the CLI (hermes cron create --help) on the current release line, Hermes Agent v0.23.2 (released 2026-11-16), rechecked 2026-11-16:

  • Schedules run in your profile's timezone (timezone: in config.yaml), not raw UTC. A job can pin its own zone: hermes cron create "0 9 * * 1-5" --timezone America/New_York "US market open brief".
  • Script-only jobs skip the model entirely: hermes cron create "every 5m" --no-agent --script memory-watchdog.sh --name memory-watchdog. Stdout is delivered verbatim, empty stdout is a silent tick, and a non-zero exit or timeout raises an alert.
  • --script is always a file, never a command line. It must resolve inside $HERMES_HOME/scripts/; --script "echo hi" is refused at creation time.
  • Catch-up is bounded: a missed occurrence runs late only inside half the job's period, clamped to 2 minutes - 2 hours. --grace-minutes (0-1440) overrides that per job.
  • Recursion is opt-in: by default a session launched by the scheduler cannot create, edit, or remove cron jobs. cron.allow_agent_scheduling: true in config.yaml lifts that, letting a scheduled agent manage the same flat jobs.json table; a job can even remove itself and still deliver its final response. Leave it off unless you actually want jobs that reschedule themselves.
  • Failure isolation: hermes cron cancel stops a run in flight without touching the job's schedule; hermes pause halts the whole fleet.

docs.title: The Cardinal Rule: Idempotency
docs.text:
Every cron should be safe to run multiple times with the same inputs. Cron schedulers can drift, containers can restart, and manual re-runs happen during debugging. If your cron writes to a database, use upsert semantics. If it sends notifications, track sent status. If it generates reports, use deterministic filenames.

A good litmus test: could you run this cron three times back-to-back without breaking anything?

docs.title: Error Handling: Fail Loudly, Recover Gracefully
docs.text:
Retry with backoff. Transient failures (network timeouts, rate limits) should retry with exponential backoff. Cap at 3-5 attempts with jitter.

Dead-letter queue. After all retries exhausted, route failed work to a dead-letter queue or structured log. Never silently discard work.

Alert on persistent failure. If your cron fails for more than N consecutive runs, trigger an alert through Slack, email, or PagerDuty.

Partial success handling. Handle individual failures within a batch without aborting the entire batch. Log failed records and continue processing.

docs.title: Rate Limiting and Delivery Targets
docs.text:
Define explicit throughput targets. Implement token-bucket or sliding-window rate limiting. Maintain separate rate-limit budgets per API integration.

Delivery windows matter. If your cron takes 4 minutes to complete, don't schedule it every 5 minutes - that leaves only 1 minute of slack. Schedule at 2-3x the expected runtime to prevent overlap.

docs.title: Monitoring and Observability
docs.text:
Every cron should emit:

  • Start/end timestamps with duration - track runtime drift
  • Record counts - items read, written, failed
  • Error counts by type
  • Last successful run timestamp - your canary

Heartbeat monitoring: A separate lightweight check every 15-30 minutes verifies the last successful run is within the expected window.

docs.title: Anti-Patterns to Avoid
docs.text: Anti-Pattern Why It Hurts Fix God Cron One failure cascades everything Split into single-responsibility crons Hardcoded timestamps DST/timezone bugs Always UTC, always timezone-aware Unbounded queries Million-row timeouts Always paginate/LIMIT Missing dry-run mode Can't test safely Add --dry-run flag Console output as logging Ephemeral, unsearchable Structured persistent logging

docs.title: Delivery Target Patterns
docs.text:
• Real-time needs: Use event-driven architecture, not polling crons
  • Near-real-time: Every 5 minutes - acceptable for most ecommerce
  • Hourly: Good for dashboards, cache warming
  • Daily: Batch windows for exports, reconciliation
  • Weekly/monthly: Run during low-traffic with explicit retry windows

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Zero silent failures: Alerting on persistent failure catches issues before users notice
  • Predictable costs: Rate limiting prevents API overage charges
  • Easy debugging: Structured logs with timestamps and record counts
  • Safe testing: Dry-run mode lets you verify changes before deployment

docs.title: What makes a cron job idempotent in Hermes Agent?
docs.text: A cron is idempotent if running it multiple times with the same inputs produces the same result. Use upsert database operations, deduplication keys on notifications, and deterministic file naming for reports.

docs.title: How many times should a failed cron retry?
docs.text: Retry 3-5 times with exponential backoff and jitter. After all retries are exhausted, route to a dead-letter queue - never silently discard work. Alert after 3 consecutive failures.

docs.title: How do I monitor cron job health?
docs.text: Track start/end timestamps, record counts processed, error counts by type, and last successful run timestamp. Run a separate heartbeat check every 15-30 minutes to catch stale crons.

docs.title: Run a Local Coding Agent: OpenCode + Nemotron on GPU
docs.text:
Frontier coding agents are powerful and expensive. Most repository work is not frontier work: conformance passes, bulk edits, small refactors, test scaffolding. Running those on a local model turns a metered cost into an electricity bill, and your code never leaves the machine.

This guide walks through a setup that works: opencode as the agent, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning served by vLLM on a DGX Spark, with the operational details that separate a demo from a tool you trust.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A machine with a modern NVIDIA GPU and enough unified or device memory for the model (a 30B model in NVFP4 fits comfortably on 128GB unified memory).
  • Docker or Podman with GPU access (CDI on recent Podman).
  • Node.js for opencode, Python for the serving stack.

docs.title: Serve the model
docs.text:
Run vLLM as a supervised service, not a manual container. A systemd unit with automatic restart is the difference between a toy and infrastructure:

podman run --rm --name nemotron-vllm \
  --device nvidia.com/gpu=all --ipc=host \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8100:8000 \
  -v /models/main:/models/main:ro \
  docker.io/vllm/vllm-openai:latest \
  --model /models/main --served-model-name nemotron-35-lightning \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --enable-prefix-caching \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.70 --max-num-seqs 16

Two flags matter more than they look. Memory utilization sets how much of the device the engine may claim. On a unified-memory box the host stack needs real headroom, and an aggressive value causes the engine to die under load, taking your agent sessions with it. Start at 0.70 and leave room. Capping concurrent sequences bounds KV cache growth when several agent loops run at once.

docs.title: Install and configure opencode
docs.text:
npm i -g opencode-ai

That installs the OpenCode 1 line, which is what the rest of this guide is written against. As of November 2026 the npm opencode-ai package still publishes the 1.x line (latest 1.19.5), and https://opencode.ai/install redirects to the v1 branch of the install script, so the one-liner and the npm path give you the same generation. The project does publish OpenCode 2 releases on GitHub, but those are a separate distribution, not the npm package. Pick one line and stay on it, because two installations can replace each other's binary.

Point it at the local endpoint in ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:

{
  "permission": { "edit": "allow", "bash": "allow" },
  "provider": {
    "local": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "Local (GPU)",
      "options": { "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1", "apiKey": "local" },
      "models": { "nemotron-35-lightning": { "name": "Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (local)" } }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: The gotcha that costs you a repository
docs.text:
When you spawn opencode from a script, a cron job, or Python instead of an interactive shell, it resolves its working directory from the inherited PWD environment variable, not from the process working directory. The writes land wherever that variable points. We learned this the hard way: a task suite meant for a sandbox clone wrote 47 files into a different repository checkout.

Always pin the directory explicitly:

env = dict(os.environ, PWD=workdir)
subprocess.run(["opencode", "run", "--dir", workdir, "-m", model, prompt],
               cwd=workdir, env=env)

After every run, verify placement (find <workdir> -name <expected-file>) and check that no other repository gained files. A one-line guard that runs git status --short on your real checkouts after each task catches misroutes immediately.

docs.title: Make it pass real tasks
docs.text:
Local models are literal. Prompts that assume context fail. Four rules close most of the gap:

  1. Name the exact output path and say to create parent directories. Without this, files appear at the repository root.
  2. End every prompt with a verification instruction and a continue-until-it-passes sentence.
  3. For bulk work, instruct a loop: list targets with grep, fix all, re-run the check until it reports zero.
  4. Put repository conventions in an AGENTS.md at the repo root; opencode reads it automatically.

docs.title: Sandbox everything
docs.text: Run task suites against fresh clones, never live repositories. Keep one runner with per-task deterministic checks, archive results per round, and treat the checker, not the agent's summary, as the source of truth. Models occasionally report success without making a single edit; state-based checks catch that instantly.

docs.title: Honest limits
docs.text: Local coding agents are strongest on mechanical and structural work: bulk edits, format conformance, repetitive refactors, test scaffolding. They are weaker on novel implementation and long-form writing. Route accordingly: local for volume, frontier for judgment, and verification gates on both.

docs.title: MCP Server Design Guide - Build Custom AI Agent Tools
docs.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers extend Hermes Agent with custom tools and data sources. Designing an MCP server well means respecting both the protocol constraints and the expectations of the Hermes community. This MCP server design guide covers tool design, error handling, performance, testing, and the full server lifecycle.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: MCP servers are how Hermes Agent connects to external systems. Each server exposes tools - typed, documented functions that the agent can call. Following MCP design best practices ensures your server is reliable, performant, and easy for the community to adopt.

docs.title: When to Build vs When to Buy
docs.text:
Build when: No existing MCP server exists for your data source, you need custom behavior, strict security demands self-hosting, or you're integrating an internal system.

Use existing when: It covers your use case and is actively maintained. Search the MCP ecosystem and skills catalog first.

Avoid building when: A simple REST API call from a skill would work. Not every integration needs an MCP server.

docs.title: Tool Design Principles
docs.text: Principle Good Bad One tool, one responsibility get_customer_profile, get_customer_billing get_customer_data (does everything) Descriptive names list_recent_orders get_data Pagination by default Always include limit/offset Unbounded responses Consistent errors {code, message, retry_after} Raw upstream errors Filter parameters list_users(role="admin", status="active") No filter support

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• Timeouts: Configurable per tool; retry transient failures with backoff
  • Graceful degradation: Return partial results with caveats when upstream is partially down
  • Rate limit awareness: Track upstream limits; return clear retry_after guidance
  • Pre-validation: Validate parameters before upstream calls to save round trips

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• Connection pooling: Reuse HTTP connections (saves 100-300ms per call)
  • Response size discipline: Filter and limit at server level
  • Bulk operations: Provide batch endpoints for multi-record operations
  • Caching with care: Document freshness guarantees

docs.title: Protocol Revision
docs.text: Target the current revision of the specification (2026-07-28, per the official schema). That revision removed the initialize handshake: there is no negotiation step any more. Every request declares its protocol version in _meta (io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion) and, on HTTP, in the MCP-Protocol-Version header; a server that does not support the requested version answers with UnsupportedProtocolVersionError listing the versions it does support, and the client retries with one of them. Servers must implement server/discover so a client can learn the supported versions before its first call. A dual-era server that still answers the legacy 2025-11-25 handshake keeps older clients working. Check the revision before publishing and state it in your README.

docs.title: Server Lifecycle
docs.text: Development → Beta (real creds, limited access, 1+ week monitoring) → Production (full monitoring, stable schemas) → Maintenance (upstream API updates, deprecation with 30+ day notice) → Sunset

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Extensible agent capabilities: Every MCP server adds new tools Hermes Agent can use
  • Community leverage: Hundreds of existing MCP servers cover common integrations
  • Type safety: Structured tool schemas mean reliable parameter passing
  • Reusable across agents: One MCP server works with any MCP-compatible agent

docs.title: Do I need to build an MCP server for every API integration?
docs.text: No. If the integration is a single API call with simple parameters, a skill step is simpler. Build an MCP server when you need multiple tools, state management, authentication handling, or want to share with the community.

docs.title: How do I handle pagination in MCP server tools?
docs.text: Always support limit/offset or cursor-based pagination for any tool that can return more than 50 items. Return pagination metadata (total count, next cursor) so callers know when more data is available.

docs.title: How do I test an MCP server before publishing?
docs.text: Point the official inspector at it: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector. It opens a UI that lists your tools and schemas and lets you call them with hand-written arguments, which catches schema mistakes that unit tests pass over. Then unit test each tool with valid/invalid inputs and edge cases, integration test against a sandbox environment, and complete a security review for credential exposure and data logging.

docs.title: Memory Management Best Practices - Persistent AI Agent Context
docs.text: Memory is what separates a stateless tool from a persistent AI assistant in Hermes Agent. But memory also consumes context, increases latency, and introduces staleness risks. These memory management best practices cover when and how to use each memory tier for optimal agent performance.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Hermes Agent layers memory instead of storing one blob. Four tiers ship with the agent, and one external provider can be added on top of them:

  • Built-in memory - MEMORY.md and USER.md, injected into every turn for free.
  • Session search - past transcripts in a local SQLite FTS5 store, queried on demand.
  • One external memory provider - Honcho, Mem0, Hindsight, Supermemory, OpenViking, Holographic, Memori, RetainDB or ByteRover, installed from the plugin catalog.
  • Skills - procedural knowledge, versioned and loaded only when relevant.

Only one external provider can be active at a time, and the built-in memory always runs alongside it. hermes memory status shows what is active, hermes memory setup runs the interactive picker, and hermes memory off disables the external provider without touching MEMORY.md or USER.md.

Organizational indexes and retrieval services that live outside Hermes - an indexing layer such as GBrain, or a separate retrieval service - sit beside these tiers. They are companion systems, not Hermes memory providers, and they carry their own sync discipline.

docs.title: The Memory Hierarchy
docs.text: Tier System Use Case Persistence Built-in MEMORY.md / USER.md Stable facts, preferences, standing conventions Every turn Peer / user model Honcho or another external provider User identity, preferences, decisions, bans Cross-session Organizational GBrain and similar indexes File/code indexing, project relationships Cross-session Conversation history session_search (SQLite FTS5) What happened in past sessions Cross-session Conversation In-session context Task continuity within current chat Ephemeral Procedural Skills Reusable workflows, tool chains Versioned

docs.title: When to Add Memory
docs.text:
Ask these questions before storing:

  • Does this fact change rarely? Stable preferences → memory. Current task focus → conversation context.
  • Is it referenced across sessions? Multi-session project → memory. One-off question → don't store.
  • Does it save meaningful context tokens? If storing saves re-explaining each session, it's worth it.
  • Is it factual or procedural? Facts → memories. Workflows → skills. Config → env vars.

docs.title: Compaction Strategies
docs.text:
When context windows fill up:

  • Sliding window: Keep last N messages verbatim; summarize older. Best for linear task-focused conversations.
  • Hierarchical summarization: Summarize sections into bullet points; summarize summaries when chain gets long.
  • Selective retention: Flag key decisions/code to "keep forever"; summarize everything else.
  • Semantic retrieval: Index conversation turns by embedding; retrieve relevant chunks on demand.

docs.title: Memory Anti-Patterns
docs.text: Anti-Pattern Why It Hurts Fix Memory as dumping ground 500 stale entries = noise Prune periodically Contradictory memories Confusion across sessions Audit for conflicts No expiration "Working on Q2 report" stale in Q3 Add implicit/project expiry Memory replacing config API keys in memory = breach Use secrets manager

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• No session amnesia: Agents remember who you are, what you're building, and what happened last session
  • Reduced re-explanation: Stable preferences stored once, referenced forever
  • Faster onboarding: Team knowledge indexed and queryable via GBrain
  • Lower token costs: Compacted context means less wasted context window

docs.title: What's the difference between Honcho and GBrain memory?
docs.text: Honcho stores peer identity - who the user is, preferences, decisions, bans. GBrain indexes organizational knowledge - where files are, what code does what, project relationships. They solve different problems and should both be used in production.

docs.title: How do I prevent my Hermes Agent memory from getting stale?
docs.text: Prune memories periodically (monthly review), add expiration to project-specific memories, audit for contradictions, and use the dream cycle (nightly consolidation) to merge duplicates and strengthen frequently accessed paths.

docs.title: Can I use just one memory system?
docs.text: You can, but you'll have gaps. Hermes allows one external memory provider at a time, so pick the one that matches your dominant need rather than stacking several; built-in memory and session search always run underneath it. A peer-modeling provider such as Honcho does not index your files, and an indexing layer such as GBrain does not answer "who is the user?" - run one external provider for user modeling and a separate index for organizational knowledge.

docs.title: Model Selection Guide - Choose the Right AI Model Every Time
docs.text: Choosing the right model for each task is one of the highest-leverage decisions you make with Hermes Agent. A well-chosen model saves latency, cost, and context - missteps waste all three. This model selection guide covers task-to-model mapping, cost optimization, local vs cloud tradeoffs, and fallback chain patterns.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Hermes Agent runs models from local Ollama, OpenRouter, Nous Portal, and direct provider APIs. Nous Portal serves 300+ models under a single subscription, and OpenRouter's catalogue lists more than 450 model IDs (464 listed on 2026-10-28). Following best practices for model selection means using the cheapest model that reliably handles each task, reserving frontier models for complex reasoning.

docs.title: The Decision Framework
docs.text:
Ask three questions before every model selection:

  1. What does the task require? - Reasoning depth, factual precision, creative generation, or tool orchestration?
  2. What is the latency budget? - Real-time interaction, batch processing, or background work?
  3. What is the cost tolerance? - Per-request budget, daily volume, or fixed monthly spend?

docs.title: Task-to-Model Mapping
docs.text: Task Type Model Tier Examples Classification & Routing Small/Lightweight Intent detection, email triage, field extraction Data Extraction & Summarization Mid-tier Meeting transcripts, action items, structured data Complex Reasoning & Code Frontier Multi-step debugging, architecture decisions Creative & Narrative Style-appropriate Brand content, brainstorming (test with audience)

docs.title: Cost Optimization Strategies
docs.text:
Caching. If 40% of your queries are variants of the same 5 intents, cache results before hitting models.

Prompt compression. Summarize conversation history before expensive calls. Strip irrelevant tool output.

Task batching. Process similar records together - many providers offer 50% discounts on batch endpoints.

Model fallback chains. Try cheapest model first → if confidence low, escalate to mid-tier → if still uncertain, invoke frontier. This "progressive enhancement" gives frontier quality on hard cases while keeping average cost low.

docs.title: Local vs Cloud: The Real Tradeoffs
docs.text:
Local models (Ollama) win when: data privacy is non-negotiable, latency must stay sub-second, high volume makes fixed hardware cost cheaper than per-token pricing. See gaming PC setup or Mac Mini setup.

Cloud models (OpenRouter/Anthropic/OpenAI) win when: you need frontier reasoning, zero infrastructure maintenance, elastic scaling. See cloud VPS setup.

Hybrid for most teams: Classify/extract with local models (free, private); reason/generate with cloud models. Configure Hermes Agent with Ollama as primary and OpenRouter as fallback.

docs.title: The Fallback Chain Pattern
docs.text:
1. Check cache - identical query answered recently? Return cached.
  2. Try primary model - send to default model for this task class
  3. Validate output - check structure, completeness, confidence
  4. Escalate if needed - retry with stronger model
  5. Track fallback rate - if >10%, primary model is too weak

docs.title: Practical Decision Tree
docs.text:
Classification/routing? → Small model
Data extraction from known formats? → Mid-tier
Summarization of medium-length text? → Mid-tier
Multi-step reasoning or debugging? → Frontier
Creative writing or brand content? → Style-appropriate (test!)
Background batch job? → Cheapest reliable model
Latency critical (sub-second)? → Local or fastest cloud
Data sensitive/regulated? → Local or approved cloud with BAA

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• 3-10x cost reduction: Use small models for 80% of routine tasks
  • Lower latency: Local models for classification give sub-second responses
  • Privacy by default: Sensitive data stays on local models
  • Frontier quality on demand: Fallback chains escalate only when needed

docs.title: When should I use a local model vs a cloud model?
docs.text: Use local models (Ollama) for classification, extraction, and data-sensitive tasks - they're free and private. Use cloud models for complex reasoning, code generation, and tasks requiring frontier capabilities. Most teams benefit from a hybrid approach.

docs.title: How do I reduce my API costs with Hermes Agent?
docs.text: Implement caching for repeated queries, use prompt compression before expensive calls, batch non-urgent tasks, and create fallback chains that try cheaper models first. Track cost per successful task, not per token.

docs.title: What's the best model for code generation?
docs.text: Frontier models carry the hard work: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5) or Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5), the GPT-5.6 variants (openai/gpt-5.6-luna, -terra, -sol), and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash) were all listed in the OpenRouter catalogue when this page was verified on 2026-10-28. For boilerplate or simple functions, a smaller coder model such as Qwen3-Coder 30B (qwen/qwen3-coder-30b-a3b-instruct) handles it at zero marginal cost when served locally. Model names rotate every few weeks, so confirm the exact ID in the /model picker instead of trusting a table.

docs.title: Prompt Caching - How an Agent Holds a 98% Cache Hit Rate
docs.text:
Prompt caching is the single largest cost lever in a long-running agent, and it is almost never a setting you turn on. A high cache hit rate falls out of how the prompt is built: a large, byte-stable prefix that gets re-sent every turn, and a small delta on top of it. Get the structure right and the hit rate sits at 96 to 99 percent by construction. Get it wrong and it collapses toward zero without any error being raised.

This page documents the mechanics and the measurement method used on a production Hermes Agent deployment (running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and V4 Pro), so you can reproduce the numbers on your own install.

docs.title: Measured result
docs.text:
Measured on a production Hermes Agent deployment over a two-day window:

Model Hit rate deepseek-flash 98.70% deepseek-v4-pro 96.81% All traffic 98.67%

The hit rate is not uniform across sessions, and the distribution is the useful part:

Percentile Hit rate Median session 98.63% 10th percentile 97.29% 90th percentile 99.24% Worst session 60.24%

Every session in the bottom tail is a short one (one to three API calls). A session that ends early never amortises the prefix it paid for, which is the whole story of the misses.

docs.title: Why 98% is structural, not tuned
docs.text:
The miss tokens come out at almost exactly one cold prefix per session:

miss tokens per session       =  one prefix  (about 47,000 tokens here)
miss share of all tokens sent =  1.33%
cache read per API call       =  about 103,000 tokens

Read that last line again. Every turn ships a prefix of roughly 100,000 tokens, and the provider charges the cached rate for about 98,700 of them. The cost driver is prefix volume, not per-token price, and the prefix is nearly free.

docs.title: Hit versus miss pricing
docs.text:
DeepSeek V4.1 bills cache hits at a small fraction of misses. Off-peak Flash pricing is $0.003 per million cached input tokens against $0.15 per million uncached - a 50x gap. Pro charges more on both sides ($0.022 cached against $0.66 uncached), so the ratio narrows to 30x while the dollar spread widens from about 15 cents to about 64 cents per million tokens.

Applied to a window where the cache covered 98.7 percent of input, the bill lands at roughly 3 to 4 percent of what the same traffic would cost uncached. That is what the hit rate buys. Anthropic's prompt caching shows the same shape at different absolute numbers: cache reads bill at roughly 10% of base input, and cache writes carry a small premium, so the crossover comes after a couple of turns rather than immediately.

docs.title: 1. Keep a large byte-stable prefix
docs.text:
System prompt, skills, memory, tool schemas and repo context belong in the prefix, and that block must not change between turns. In the deployment measured here that block is roughly 45,000 tokens and is identical call to call. Cache lookup is a prefix match: the moment any byte inside the block changes, everything from that byte onward is a miss.

Practical consequence: put volatile content (timestamps, run IDs, "current time is...") at the end of the prompt, never in the system block. A single datetime.now() interpolation in a system prompt guarantees a permanent zero percent hit rate.

docs.title: 2. Run long sessions and amortise the cold start
docs.text:
A cold start costs one full prefix prefill. Spread over 100 turns it is noise; spread over two turns it is the entire session cost. The measured worst sessions are 1 to 3 calls at 60 to 68 percent, and they exist because cron jobs and one-shot scripts open a fresh session to ask one question.

Practical consequence: for repetitive background work, prefer a no_agent script over an agent session. A script costs zero tokens and pays no cold prefix.

docs.title: 3. Never mutate the prefix mid-session
docs.text:
These four actions all rewrite the cached prefix and turn into a miss spike:

  • Switching model mid-session (different cache namespace entirely)
  • Reloading configuration, which rebuilds the system block
  • Adding a skill or tool after turn one, which changes the tool schema region
  • Context compression, which rewrites history

One compression event per long session is free. Five in one session is a miss pump. If a session must load extra skills, load them in the first turn so the prefix stabilises once.

docs.title: 4. Respect the cache TTL on idle gaps
docs.text:
Caches expire. Anthropic's short-lived tier is around five minutes by default, extendable; DeepSeek's automatic prefix cache tolerates longer idle gaps but is not permanent. An agent that thinks for 20 minutes, takes one call, then thinks again, re-prefills on every call.

Practical consequence: batch work into continuous bursts rather than spreading the same calls across hours, if latency allows.

docs.title: Measuring cache hit rate on your own install
docs.text:
Hermes records per-session, per-model token usage in the profile's state.db. Nothing here requires an API key or a dashboard.

-- Overall hit rate by model
select model,
       sum(api_call_count)                     as calls,
       sum(input_tokens)                       as miss_tokens,
       sum(cache_read_tokens)                  as hit_tokens,
       round(100.0 * sum(cache_read_tokens)
             / (sum(cache_read_tokens) + sum(input_tokens)), 2) as hit_pct
from session_model_usage
group by model
order by sum(cache_read_tokens) desc;

-- Sessions where the hit rate is worst: your cold-start offenders
select session_id, model, api_call_count, input_tokens, cache_read_tokens,
       round(100.0 * cache_read_tokens
             / (cache_read_tokens + input_tokens), 1) as hit_pct
from session_model_usage
where input_tokens + cache_read_tokens > 5000
order by hit_pct asc
limit 10;

sqlite3 -readonly ~/.hermes/profiles/<profile>/state.db \
  "select model, sum(api_call_count), sum(input_tokens), sum(cache_read_tokens) \
   from session_model_usage group by model;"

Three readings matter:

  1. Miss tokens divided by session count. If that number is close to your prefix size, the caching is healthy and every miss is a legitimate cold start.
  2. The bottom 10 percent of sessions. Confirm they are short sessions. If they are long sessions, something is mutating the prefix and needs finding.
  3. Cache read per call. A rising value means the prefix is growing (more skills, more memory, longer history) and is the earliest warning that cost per turn is drifting up.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Chasing the hit rate instead of protecting the prefix. A hit rate is an outcome. The actions that improve it are structural: longer sessions, stable prefix, no mid-session mutation, fewer cold starts.

Putting a timestamp in the system prompt. The classic silent failure. The agent works perfectly and every single call is a full-price prefill.

Compressing aggressively on short sessions. Compression on a session that is about to end rewrites the prefix for no benefit. Compress at natural boundaries on long sessions.

Assuming caching is off because the invoice is high. At a billion tokens of monthly traffic, an invoice that looks large is usually volume, not a caching failure. Multiply tokens by the miss price to see what the cache is already saving you.

docs.title: Is prompt caching automatically enabled in Hermes Agent?
docs.text: Yes for providers that support it. Hermes sends a stable prefix and does not strip the cache markers, so both Anthropic-style explicit caching and DeepSeek-style automatic prefix caching engage without configuration. The variable is your prompt structure, not a flag.

docs.title: What cache hit rate should I expect?
docs.text: Long agent sessions with a stable prefix typically land between 96 and 99 percent. Anything under 90 percent on sessions longer than ten calls points to prefix mutation. One to three call sessions will always look poor and are not worth optimising individually.

docs.title: Does prompt caching work with local models?
docs.text: Local inference servers have their own prefix caching, and it changes the economics differently: cached prefill saves latency rather than money. The structural rules are identical, so a prompt built for a cloud cache is also a fast local prompt.

docs.title: Why is the hit rate higher on the cheaper model?
docs.text: Two reasons: high-volume daily work runs long sessions on the cheap model, and the expensive model gets the interrupted, sensitive tasks that are more likely to be one-off. Route the boring volume to the model with the longest sessions.

docs.title: Security Best Practices - Protect Your Hermes Agent Deployment
docs.text: Hermes Agent connects to your data, executes code, and runs scheduled tasks - all capabilities that require thoughtful security design. These security best practices cover credential management, approval gates, audit logging, and the patterns that prevent the most common security failures in production AI agent deployments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Security with Hermes Agent follows the least-privilege principle: start read-only, add write capabilities only with explicit approval gates, and log everything. Each connector to external services (email, CRM, databases) is a potential attack surface - managing tokens and permissions correctly is non-negotiable.

docs.title: What Hermes enforces natively
docs.text:
Verified against the official security documentation on Hermes Agent v0.23.2, checked 2026-11-16. The model has eight layers: user authorization, dangerous-command approval, file-write safety, container isolation, MCP credential filtering, context-file scanning, cross-session isolation, and input sanitization. The approval layer is configuration, not advice - set it deliberately in ~/.hermes/config.yaml:

approvals:
  mode: smart              # smart | manual | off
  timeout: 300             # seconds to wait for a human reply
  cron_mode: deny          # deny | approve - unattended cron runs
  single_query_mode: deny  # deny | approve - one-shot `hermes chat -q`
  unattended_mode: deny    # deny | approve - webhook / API sessions

The three unattended modes default to deny. That is the safe default: a cron job, one-shot query or webhook session that trips a dangerous-command prompt is blocked, and the agent has to find another path instead of auto-approving its way through. Leave them at deny unless you have a specific, documented reason.

Below the approval layer sits a floor nothing lifts: a fixed hardline blocklist (rm -rf / and its variants, fork bombs, mkfs on a mounted root device, dd onto a block device, Windows format/recursive-drive-wipe commands, piping untrusted URLs to a root shell). --yolo, /yolo, approvals.mode: off and a headless approve cron mode all walk around the prompts but never around that list - the call returns an error and nothing runs. For your own exceptions there is approvals.deny, a list of glob patterns blocked before any of those bypasses are consulted:

approvals:
  deny:
    - "git push --force*"
    - "*curl*|*sh*"
    - "dd if=* of=/dev/*"

Patterns are case-insensitive fnmatch globs matched against the whole command and against each executable candidate, and they follow the same de-obfuscation the dangerous-pattern detector uses. Always quote them: a bare leading * is a YAML alias and the file will not parse.

docs.title: Credential Management
docs.text:
Never hardcode credentials in skills, crons, or prompt templates. Use environment variables or a secrets manager. A skill reading api_key = "sk-abc123" is a breach waiting to happen.

Least privilege for every connector. Grant only the permissions Hermes Agent actually needs. Read-only Gmail scope, SELECT-only database role, scoped API keys with explicit boundaries.

Rotate credentials quarterly. Document rotation procedures so it's a 5-minute task, not a fire drill.

No shared API keys. Each team member needs their own credentials for audit trails and individual revocation.

docs.title: Tiered Approval Gates
docs.text: Tier Type Approval Required Examples Tier 0 Read-only None Queries, reports, analysis Tier 1 Internal write One-click confirm Draft docs, internal notes Tier 2 External write Explicit confirmation + preview Sending emails, posting messages Tier 3 High-impact Multi-step with reason capture Financial transactions, bulk changes

docs.title: Audit Logging
docs.text: Log every significant action: what was done, by whom, when, with what inputs, and the result. Use structured logging (JSON), not free-text. Store logs in append-only storage for 30-90 days minimum. Schedule weekly log reviews or set up automated anomaly detection.

docs.title: Secrets and Sensitive Data
docs.text: Never store in memory/context: API keys, passwords, credit card numbers, PII, auth tokens, private keys. Strip sensitive fields before data enters model context. Redact PII in logs.

docs.title: Operational Security Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] All credentials in secrets manager, never in version control
  • [ ] Each connector uses scoped, least-privilege credentials
  • [ ] Write operations require confirmation gates
  • [ ] Audit logging enabled and reviewed weekly
  • [ ] Sensitive data stripped before model context
  • [ ] Community skills reviewed before installation
  • [ ] Credentials rotate on documented schedule
  • [ ] Logs stored append-only and immutable
  • [ ] Anomalous activity triggers alerts

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Breach prevention: Hardened credential management eliminates the #1 attack vector
  • Compliance ready: Audit logging satisfies SOC 2, HIPAA, and internal review requirements
  • Safe automation: Approval gates let you automate writes without losing control
  • Revocable access: Individual credentials mean you can cut off one user without disrupting the team

docs.title: How do I manage API keys securely with Hermes Agent?
docs.text: Never hardcode keys in skills or prompts. Use environment variables, a secrets manager, or the built-in credential store. Each connector should use scoped keys with only the permissions Hermes Agent needs - prefer read-only where possible.

docs.title: What actions require human approval in Hermes Agent?
docs.text: Any write operation that affects external systems: sending emails, updating CRM records, modifying databases, posting to Slack, executing financial transactions. Configure tiered approval gates appropriate to the risk level.

docs.title: How often should I rotate Hermes Agent credentials?
docs.text: Rotate API keys and tokens quarterly at minimum. Document the rotation procedure for each connector so it's a quick task. Set calendar reminders - expired tokens are the #1 cause of silent automation failures.
