docs.title: Gaming PC Hermes Agent Setup - CUDA-Accelerated AI Workstation
docs.text: Got a gaming rig with an NVIDIA GPU? It's a perfect Hermes Agent host for developers and power users. Run models locally at full speed with CUDA acceleration - no per-token API costs, no latency, no rate limits. This gaming PC setup guide covers everything from NVIDIA drivers to persistent operation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A gaming PC delivers the highest raw inference performance for local AI models. With 8-24GB of VRAM and CUDA acceleration, you can run models from 7B to 70B parameters locally at 50-200 tokens per second. Combined with Hermes Agent's model selection capabilities, you get a powerful AI workstation.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Feature Gaming PC Advantage GPU memory 8-24GB VRAM (runs 7B-70B models) Inference speed 50-200 tokens/sec with CUDA Cost per token $0.00 (electricity only) Multi-GPU Possible with NVLink Existing hardware You already own it

docs.title: Minimum Specs
docs.text:
• GPU: NVIDIA GTX 1060 (6GB) or better - RTX 3060+ recommended
  • RAM: 16GB system memory minimum, 32GB+ ideal
  • Storage: 50GB free for models and embeddings
  • OS: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04/24.04) or Windows 11 + WSL2

docs.title: Step 1: NVIDIA Drivers + CUDA
docs.text:
# Ubuntu 24.04
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nvidia-driver-550 nvidia-cuda-toolkit

# Verify
nvidia-smi

docs.title: Step 2: Install Ollama with GPU Acceleration
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama run llama3.2 "say hello"
# Check: nvidia-smi should show ollama using GPU memory

docs.title: Step 3: Pull Models That Fit Your VRAM
docs.text:
# 6-8GB VRAM: 7B-8B models
ollama pull llama3.2          # ~4.7GB
ollama pull mistral:7b         # ~4.1GB

# 12-16GB VRAM: 13B-14B models
ollama pull qwen2.5:14b        # ~8.5GB
ollama pull phi4:14b           # ~9.1GB

# 20-24GB VRAM: 32B-34B models
ollama pull qwen2.5:32b        # ~20GB
ollama pull codestral:22b      # ~13GB

# Embeddings (always pull)
ollama pull nomic-embed-text   # ~274MB

docs.title: Step 4: Install Hermes Agent
docs.text:
# Official installer - brings its own pinned Python and toolchain
curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash

hermes profile create gpu-agent
hermes profile use gpu-agent
hermes config set model.provider ollama
hermes config set model.default qwen2.5:14b    # provider-relative - no "ollama/" prefix
hermes fallback add    # cloud fallback, tried on rate-limit/overload/connection errors

docs.title: Step 5: Maximize GPU Performance
docs.text:
# Set GPU to persistence mode
sudo nvidia-smi -pm 1

# Ollama optimization
export OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1
export OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1
export OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=10m

docs.title: Step 6: Persistent Operation
docs.text:
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/hermes-gateway.service << 'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Hermes Agent Gateway
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=your-username
ExecStart=/home/your-username/.local/bin/hermes gateway run
Restart=always
RestartSec=10
Environment=HOME=/home/your-username

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

sudo systemctl enable --now hermes-gateway

docs.title: Step 7: Browser Automation
docs.text:
# Hermes installs a pinned Chromium for local browsing; verify it is healthy
hermes doctor
sudo apt install libnvidia-gl-550  # For headless GPU rendering

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Zero API costs: All inference runs locally on your GPU
  • Maximum speed: 50-200 tokens/sec with CUDA
  • Complete privacy: Models and data never leave your machine
  • No rate limits: Unlimited inference 24/7
  • Multi-GPU ready: Scale with NVLink for larger models
  • Flexible fallback: Add cloud models via OpenRouter for frontier capabilities

docs.title: Windows + WSL2 Alternative
docs.text: If you game on Windows, follow the WSL2 guide. GPU passthrough works - Ollama inside WSL2 sees your NVIDIA GPU via nvidia-smi.

docs.title: Can my gaming PC run Hermes Agent while I'm gaming?
docs.text: Yes. Set OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=10m so models unload from VRAM when idle. During gaming, Hermes Agent can use cloud fallback models or wait until you're done.

docs.title: What VRAM do I need for local LLMs?
docs.text: 6-8GB VRAM handles 7B models. 12-16GB handles 13-14B models. 24GB handles 32B models. See our model selection guide for detailed recommendations.

docs.title: Which GPU is best for Hermes Agent?
docs.text: Any RTX 30-series or newer works well. The RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM) is ideal for running 32B+ models. Multiple GPUs can be combined with NVLink.

docs.title: Mac Mini M4 AI Server Setup: Ollama, MLX, Playwright
docs.text: The Mac Mini M4 is the ideal single-machine Hermes Agent host for solo founders and developers. Everything runs on one box: LLM inference with Ollama and MLX, browser automation with Playwright, cron scheduling, and messaging - no worker nodes, no SSH keys, no multi-machine complexity.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Mac Mini M4's unified memory architecture (16-32GB shared CPU/GPU) makes it uniquely suited for running local AI models. Combined with silent operation (~20W idle) and native macOS support for Playwright browser automation, it's the recommended Hermes Agent setup platform for solo operators who want a single-box solution.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Component How It Runs on Mac Mini M4 Local Models Ollama + MLX; up to ~13B parameters comfortably with 16GB RAM Cloud Models OpenRouter or direct Anthropic/OpenAI/DeepSeek API access Browser Automation Playwright runs natively on macOS; patchright for Cloudflare-bypass Memory Honcho (peer memory), GBrain (project knowledge), memcore-cloud (cross-session) Crons Hermes cron scheduler with launchd for auto-restart Messaging 21+ messaging platforms - 19 native to the gateway (Telegram, Slack, Discord, WhatsApp, Signal, SMS, Matrix, ...) plus IRC and Microsoft Teams through plugins

docs.title: Step 1: macOS Prerequisites
docs.text:
Tier-1 support on macOS is Apple Silicon. Intel Macs are best-effort only: pip install is not a supported install method for any platform, and Intel desktop bundles ship only for releases cut with --with macos-intel. The installer brings its own pinned Python 3.14, Node.js, ripgrep and FFmpeg, so Homebrew is only needed for extras.

# Install Homebrew if you don't have it
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

# Optional extras
brew install ffmpeg git

docs.title: Step 2: Install Hermes Agent
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash
source ~/.zshrc
hermes --version

docs.title: Step 3: Model Setup
docs.text:
Pick one or both strategies:

Local Models (Ollama - Free):

# Install Ollama
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

# Pull models
ollama pull llama3.2          # Lightweight daily driver
ollama pull nomic-embed-text   # Embeddings for memory
ollama pull qwen2.5:14b        # Heavier tasks (if 24GB+ RAM)

# Configure Hermes to use Ollama
hermes config set model.provider ollama
hermes config set model.default llama3.2

Cloud Models (OpenRouter - Pay-per-use):

hermes config set OPENROUTER_API_KEY "your-key"   # written to ~/.hermes/.env
hermes model                                      # pick provider + default model

Model ids are provider-relative: llama3.2 under ollama, anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6 under openrouter. Do not prefix the id with the provider name. For a fallback chain, edit fallback_providers in config.yaml (a YAML list that hermes config set cannot build).

Strategy: Use local models for cron tasks and embeddings (free), cloud models for complex reasoning (pay-as-you-go). Set Ollama as primary and OpenRouter as fallback, or vice versa depending on budget. See our model selection guide for detailed tiering strategies.

docs.title: Step 4: Browser Automation
docs.text:
Playwright runs directly on the Mac. No worker node needed.

pip install playwright
playwright install chromium

# Test
python3 -c "from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright; print('OK')"

For sites with Cloudflare protection, add patchright:

pip install patchright
patchright install chromium

docs.title: Step 5: Social Publishing (Postiz)
docs.text:
npm install -g postiz               # npm package is `postiz` (bin: postiz)
postiz auth:login                   # OAuth2 device flow; or export POSTIZ_API_KEY
# → Opens browser: log in and authorize platform connectors

docs.title: Step 6: Persistent Operation
docs.text:
Gateway (Background):

# Install as a launchd service (auto-restart, starts on login)
hermes gateway install --start-now

# Verify
hermes gateway status

Cron Jobs:

# Email monitoring every 15 minutes
hermes cron create "*/15 * * * *" \
  "Check inbox for unread. Summarize new emails. Silent if empty." \
  --name "email-watch"

# Daily summary at 6 PM
hermes cron create "0 18 * * *" \
  "Summarize today's activity. What happened? What's pending?" \
  --name "daily-report"

See cron design best practices for production-grade scheduling patterns.

Keep Alive:

Prevent macOS sleep during operation:

# Keep system awake while Hermes runs
caffeinate -dims &

Or go to System Settings → Battery → Options → Prevent automatic sleeping on power adapter.

docs.title: Step 7: Memory Stack
docs.text:
# Honcho - peer memory (2 min)
# --auth header prompts for the bearer token and writes it to ~/.hermes/.env
# (--args always comes last: it takes everything that follows)
hermes mcp add honcho --auth header --command npx --args mcp-remote https://mcp.honcho.dev

# GBrain - project memory (10 min)
git clone https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain && cd gbrain && ./setup.sh

# Cross-session plugins come from the curated catalog
hermes plugins search memory
hermes plugins install <name>          # then: hermes plugins enable <name>

Full details in the memory architecture guide.

docs.title: Benefits of Mac Mini M4 + Hermes Agent
docs.text:
• Single-box simplicity: No worker nodes, no SSH, no multi-machine coordination
  • Unified memory: 16-32GB shared between CPU and GPU - ideal for local LLM inference
  • Silent operation: ~20W idle, ~40W under load - leave it running 24/7
  • Native browser automation: Playwright and patchright run directly on macOS
  • Developer ecosystem: Homebrew, Python, Node.js - everything just works
  • Cost efficiency: $599 one-time hardware, free local models, ~$3/month electricity

docs.title: Cost Summary
docs.text:
Item Cost Mac Mini M4 hardware $599 (one-time) Ollama models Free OpenRouter API ~$5-20/month Honcho Free tier available Electricity ~$3/month at $0.15/kWh

Total: ~$600 upfront, $10-25/month ongoing.

docs.title: Why is Mac Mini M4 recommended over a gaming PC?
docs.text: The Mac Mini M4 offers silent operation, lower power consumption (~20W vs 150W+), unified memory architecture that's ideal for LLM inference, and native macOS support for all Hermes Agent features. A gaming PC setup provides more raw GPU power but at higher cost, noise, and power draw.

docs.title: Can I use only local models on Mac Mini?
docs.text: Yes. With 16GB RAM you can comfortably run models up to ~8B parameters; with 24GB+ you can run 13B-14B models. For heavier workloads, supplement with cloud models via OpenRouter as a fallback.

docs.title: How do I prevent my Mac Mini from sleeping?
docs.text: Use caffeinate -dims & from the terminal or go to System Settings → Battery → Options → Prevent automatic sleeping on power adapter.

docs.title: What if I need more GPU power?
docs.text: Add a gaming PC worker node via SSH for GPU-heavy inference, or use cloud GPU instances for burst workloads.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi 5 Hermes Agent Setup - Ultra-Low-Cost 24/7 AI Agent
docs.text: Run Hermes Agent 24/7 on a Raspberry Pi 5 for less than $80 in hardware and pennies a month in electricity. This Raspberry Pi setup guide is perfect for email monitoring, lightweight cron jobs, and home automation agents that run silently and cost almost nothing.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Raspberry Pi 5 is the most cost-effective always-on Hermes Agent platform. At $50-80, it draws ~5W idle and costs ~$5/year in electricity. It pairs with cloud API models for AI capabilities and is ideal for lightweight, persistent automation tasks that don't require GPU acceleration.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Feature Raspberry Pi 5 Cost $50-80 (board only) Power draw ~5W idle, ~10W under load Annual electricity ~$5-10 (24/7 at $0.12/kWh) RAM 4GB, 8GB or 16GB Storage microSD or NVMe (via HAT) Noise Silent (no fan needed for light loads)

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No GPU acceleration for local LLMs - use API-based cloud models or very small quantized models
  • RAM ceiling - even the 16GB board is far short of what a 7B+ model needs, so keep inference on cloud APIs or 1-2B quantized models locally
  • ARM64 architecture - some packages may need workarounds

docs.title: Step 1: OS Setup
docs.text:
# Flash Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit) with Pi Imager
# Enable SSH, set username/password, configure WiFi

# SSH in after first boot:
ssh pi@raspberrypi.local
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

docs.title: Step 2: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv git curl
# Node 26 is the current LTS line (LTS since October 2026); Node 24 stays in maintenance until April 2028
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_26.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt install -y nodejs

docs.title: Step 3: Install Hermes Agent
docs.text:
# Official installer - provisions its own pinned Python and toolchain,
# so no system pip or venv setup is required on the Pi
curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash

hermes profile create pi-agent
hermes profile use pi-agent

docs.title: Step 4: Model Strategy
docs.text:
Primary: Cloud Models (Recommended)

hermes config set OPENROUTER_API_KEY "your-key"
# any listed OpenRouter model id works; qwen3-235b-a22b-2507 is a cheap general-purpose pick
hermes config set model.default openrouter/qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507

Optional: Tiny Local Models

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama pull tinyllama       # ~637MB, runs on 4GB Pi
ollama pull nomic-embed-text # Embeddings
# Expect 2-5 tokens/sec - slow but functional

docs.title: Step 5: External Storage (Recommended)
docs.text:
# NVMe via HAT or USB SSD
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/ssd
sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/ssd
mkdir -p /mnt/ssd/hermes-data
export HERMES_HOME=/mnt/ssd/hermes-data
echo 'export HERMES_HOME=/mnt/ssd/hermes-data' >> ~/.bashrc

docs.title: Step 6: Headless Operation
docs.text:
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/hermes-gateway.service << 'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Hermes Agent Gateway
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=pi
ExecStart=/home/pi/.local/bin/hermes gateway run
Restart=always
RestartSec=15
Environment=HOME=/home/pi
Environment=HERMES_HOME=/mnt/ssd/hermes-data

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now hermes-gateway

docs.title: Step 7: Lightweight Crons
docs.text:
# Email check - uses cloud model, no local compute
# schedule and prompt are positional; --name is a flag
hermes cron create "*/30 * * * *" \
  "Check for new emails. Summarize in one sentence." \
  --name email-watch

# System health - light, local-only
hermes cron create "0 * * * *" \
  "Check temperature, disk, memory. Report if >80%." \
  --name pi-health

docs.title: Step 8: Cooling and Power
docs.text:
vcgencmd measure_temp
# If exceeding 70°C, add active cooler (~$5)
# Use 5V 5A power supply - undervoltage causes crashes

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Lowest cost: Under $100 hardware, ~$5/month ongoing
  • Silent 24/7: No fan needed, ~5W power draw
  • Perfect for monitoring: Email, cron jobs, system health checks
  • Zero maintenance: Headless operation with systemd auto-restart
  • Privacy: Runs entirely on your local network

docs.title: Cost Summary
docs.text: Item Cost Raspberry Pi 5 (4GB) $50 Power supply + case $15 microSD (32GB) $8 NVMe SSD (optional) $25 Total hardware ~$75-100 Electricity (annual) ~$6 OpenRouter API $0-5/month

docs.title: When Not to Use a Pi
docs.text:
• Heavy browser automation (Playwright struggles)
  • Running models larger than 1-2B parameters locally
  • Video processing or encoding
  • Multi-agent fleets

For those workloads, use a cloud VPS or gaming PC.

docs.title: Can a Raspberry Pi run local AI models?
docs.text: Only very small models like TinyLlama (~1B parameters). Expect 2-5 tokens/second. For practical AI, use cloud API models via OpenRouter - free tier models cost $0/token.

docs.title: Why use external storage with Raspberry Pi?
docs.text: microSD cards wear out under constant write operations from logs and memory systems. An NVMe SSD via HAT or USB SSD provides faster, more durable storage.

docs.title: What tasks is a Raspberry Pi best for with Hermes Agent?
docs.text: Email monitoring, system health checks, lightweight cron jobs, IoT automation, and notification routing. Not suitable for browser automation, video processing, or heavy inference.

docs.title: Delete Hermes Agent Sessions and Prune state.db
docs.text:
Every Hermes Agent conversation is a session stored in state.db, a SQLite database in your Hermes home. Sessions accumulate as you work, and the file grows with them. Hermes ships the commands to list sessions, delete one, prune a date range, archive instead of deleting, and reclaim the disk space afterwards. None of them require a plugin.

The short version:

hermes sessions list --limit 20                    # see what is there
hermes sessions delete <session-id>                # remove one session
hermes sessions prune --older-than 30 --dry-run    # preview a range
hermes sessions prune --older-than 30              # delete that range
hermes sessions optimize                           # reclaim the space

docs.title: What each command does
docs.text: Command Effect Changes data hermes sessions list Recent sessions with title, workspace, last active time and ID No hermes sessions stats Session and message counts, plus current database size No hermes sessions export Writes sessions out to JSONL, Markdown, QMD, HTML or a trace file No hermes sessions delete <id> Deletes one session Yes hermes sessions prune Deletes every session matching the filters you pass Yes hermes sessions archive Soft-hides matching sessions and keeps the data Yes hermes sessions pin <id> Marks sessions as keep, exempt from the stale sweep and from prune Yes hermes sessions optimize Merges search-index segments and VACUUMs the database Reclaims space

docs.title: Delete a single session
docs.text:
List first, then delete by ID:

hermes sessions list --limit 20
hermes sessions delete local-9b97db23af8d03f7d4150d45a222a82956cdca462efc51a5ba5dc4e6ef222822

delete asks for confirmation unless you pass --yes. There is no undo, so export anything you may want later first.

docs.title: Prune a range of sessions
docs.text:
prune takes the same filters you would expect from a log rotation tool:

Flag Matches --older-than AGE Last active more than AGE ago. Bare numbers are days; 12h, 2d and 1w also work --newer-than AGE Last active within the last AGE --before / --after An ISO timestamp boundary --source One source, for example cli, telegram or discord --title Sessions whose title contains a substring --min-messages / --max-messages Session size in messages --min-tokens / --max-tokens, --min-cost / --max-cost Spent budget per session --min-tool-calls / --max-tool-calls Tool call count --include-archived, --include-pinned Widen the match to archived or pinned sessions

The older filters are the ones people use most, but the full set also covers --end-reason, --cwd, --model, --provider, --user, --chat-id, --chat-type, --branch and --never-active. hermes sessions prune --help prints the current list.

Two defaults are worth knowing before you run it. A bare hermes sessions prune with no filters assumes --older-than 90, and any filter you pass matches sessions of every age. That second rule is the one that surprises people, so use --dry-run:

hermes sessions prune --older-than 30 --dry-run

A dry run prints the cutoff and the match count without writing anything. When the count looks right, run the same command without --dry-run and add --yes to skip the prompt.

docs.title: Archive instead of delete
docs.text:
hermes sessions archive takes the same filters, does the same matching and writes nothing destructive. Archived sessions stay in the database and drop out of the default listing, which is what you want for sessions you may need to read again. They come back into scope with --include-archived.

Use pin for the opposite intent. A pinned session is exempt from the stale sweep and from prune:

hermes sessions pin <session-id>
hermes sessions pinned

docs.title: Reclaim the disk space
docs.text:
Deleting rows does not shrink a SQLite file. The pages stay allocated and are reused by later writes, so the file only gets smaller after a VACUUM. hermes sessions optimize merges the search-index segments and runs the VACUUM in one step. It changes no data.

Run it when nothing else is holding the database:

hermes gateway stop
hermes sessions optimize
hermes gateway start

The gateway, the desktop app, the dashboard and the cron dispatcher all keep state.db open. Optimize refuses to run while another Hermes process holds the file, and --force overrides that refusal. The command's own help states the risk plainly: rewriting the store under a live writer can leave every agent refusing turns until all writers are stopped. Stop the writers, then optimize.

Two related stores are separate from state.db and have their own commands:

  • hermes sessions optimize-storage migrates the search index to the compact v23 layout, which reclaims space on large databases without touching session content.
  • hermes checkpoints status reports the filesystem checkpoint store, the shadow git repo that snapshots working directories before file edits. hermes checkpoints prune deletes orphaned checkpoints and garbage-collects the store, and hermes checkpoints clear wipes the rollback history entirely.

docs.title: Safety checklist
docs.text:
1. Run hermes sessions stats to record the size you are starting from.
  2. Run the delete or prune you intend with --dry-run and read the match count.
  3. Export anything you might need: hermes sessions export --format jsonl sessions.jsonl. The md and qmd formats write one file per session, so they take a directory rather than a filename.
  4. Pin the sessions you want to survive a future sweep.
  5. Delete or prune without --dry-run.
  6. Optimize in a quiet window, with the gateway stopped.
  7. Run hermes sessions stats again to confirm the file shrank.

docs.title: What deletion does and does not touch
docs.text: Deleting a session removes that session and its messages from the session store. It does not touch your configuration, your skills, your cron jobs, your memory files, or the checkpoint store. Those live in separate paths under your Hermes home, and each has its own management command.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Does deleting sessions reduce token cost? No. Tokens are model usage, not storage. Deleting sessions frees disk space only.

Why does state.db stay the same size after I delete sessions? SQLite does not return freed pages to the filesystem until a VACUUM. Run hermes sessions optimize.

Can I undo a delete? No. Deletion is permanent. Archive keeps the session and hides it instead, and an export gives you a file you can keep.

Do archived sessions still count toward database size? Yes. Archiving hides a session from the default listing, it does not remove the data. Prune them when you no longer need them.

Does prune delete my current session? Prune matches on last-active time, so a session you are actively using falls outside an --older-than window. Read the dry run before you confirm.

Is it safe to run while the gateway is up? Listing, stats and export are read-only and safe at any time. Delete and prune are ordinary writes and safe while the gateway runs. Optimize is the one command that needs the writers stopped.

docs.title: Windows 11 WSL2 Hermes Agent Setup - Linux AI Agent on Windows
docs.text: Run Hermes Agent on Windows 11 with full Linux compatibility via WSL2 - no dual-booting required. Get NVIDIA GPU acceleration for local models through CUDA passthrough, native Linux filesystem performance, and all Hermes Agent features. This Windows WSL2 setup guide covers everything from installation to persistent 24/7 operation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: WSL2 provides a real Linux kernel inside Windows, enabling Hermes Agent to run exactly as it would on a native Linux machine. GPU passthrough means your NVIDIA card accelerates Ollama models at full CUDA speed. The setup is free if you already own a Windows PC, making it the easiest entry point for Windows users who want the full Hermes Agent setup experience.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Feature WSL2 Benefit Linux kernel Real Linux, not emulation GPU passthrough NVIDIA CUDA works inside WSL2 Filesystem ext4 inside, accessible from Windows via \\wsl$ Networking Shared with Windows - no VM networking hassle Systemd Supported - run Hermes Agent as a service

docs.title: Step 1: Install WSL2
docs.text:
Open PowerShell as Administrator:

wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04
# Set up Linux username/password after reboot
wsl --list --verbose

docs.title: Step 2: Configure WSL2 Resources
docs.text:
Create %USERPROFILE%\.wslconfig:

[wsl2]
memory=8GB
processors=4
swap=4GB
networkingMode=mirrored

Apply: wsl --shutdown in PowerShell, then reopen WSL.

docs.title: Step 3: GPU Passthrough (NVIDIA)
docs.text:
Install the latest NVIDIA Windows display driver for your GPU - that single install maps CUDA into WSL:

# Download the GeForce / RTX production driver for your GPU from https://www.nvidia.com/drivers/
# Not the CUDA toolkit, and no Linux driver is involved

Inside WSL, confirm the mapping instead of installing a driver:

nvidia-smi   # Should show your GPU (WSL exposes a reduced feature set)

Do not install a Linux NVIDIA driver inside WSL. nvidia-utils-*, cuda-drivers and nvidia-open overwrite the driver mapped in from Windows and break CUDA; install only the CUDA Toolkit packages if you need to compile.

docs.title: Step 4: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
The Hermes installer provisions its own pinned Python 3.14, Node.js, ripgrep and FFmpeg, so you only need the base utilities:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git curl tar ffmpeg

Install Node.js separately only if your own tooling needs a system-wide copy:

# Node 26 is the current LTS line (LTS since October 2026)
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_26.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt install -y nodejs

docs.title: Step 5: Install Hermes Agent
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash
source ~/.bashrc
hermes profile create wsl-agent
hermes profile use wsl-agent
hermes setup                              # provider, API keys, model

To set values non-interactively:

hermes config set OPENROUTER_API_KEY sk-or-...   # written to ~/.hermes/.env
hermes model                                     # interactive provider + model picker

docs.title: Step 6: Local Models with Ollama
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama pull llama3.2
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
ollama pull qwen2.5:14b  # If 12GB+ VRAM
ollama run llama3.2                            # Loads the model
ollama ps                                      # PROCESSOR column shows the GPU/CPU split

docs.title: Step 7: Filesystem Strategy
docs.text:
Location Speed Best For /home/ (Linux ext4) Fast Hermes config, skills, crons /mnt/c/ (Windows NTFS) Slower Shared files, backups

Rule: Keep active Hermes data in /home/ for performance. For model selection and memory, WSL2's ext4 filesystem is significantly faster than NTFS.

docs.title: Step 8: Systemd Service
docs.text:
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/hermes-gateway.service << 'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Hermes Agent Gateway
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=your-username
ExecStart=/home/your-username/.local/bin/hermes gateway run
Restart=always
RestartSec=10
Environment=HOME=/home/your-username

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now hermes-gateway

docs.title: Step 9: Keep WSL2 Running
docs.text:
WSL2 shuts down when idle. Prevent this:

# Task Scheduler → Create Task → Trigger: At startup
# Action: wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-24.04 -e sleep infinity

docs.title: Step 10: Browser Automation
docs.text:
pip install playwright
playwright install chromium
playwright install-deps chromium

For headed browsing, install a Windows X server like VcXsrv and export DISPLAY=:0.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Free: No additional hardware needed beyond your Windows PC
  • Full GPU acceleration: NVIDIA CUDA works natively inside WSL2
  • No dual-boot: Run Linux Hermes Agent alongside Windows apps
  • Local models: Ollama at full speed via GPU passthrough
  • Persistent: Systemd service with auto-restart keeps Hermes alive

docs.title: Does Ollama GPU acceleration work in WSL2?
docs.text: Yes. NVIDIA's WSL2 driver enables full CUDA passthrough. Ollama detects the GPU automatically and uses it for inference - same speed as native Linux.

docs.title: Why not just use Windows native Hermes Agent?
docs.text: Native Windows is supported: grab the MSIX desktop package, or run iex (irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1) in PowerShell for a command-line install. WSL2 is still the better fit for 24/7 server-style operation because it gives you systemd, an ext4 filesystem, and native Linux package management, and many MCP servers and developer tools assume Linux. Pick native Windows for the desktop app, WSL2 for an always-on agent host.

docs.title: How do I prevent WSL2 from shutting down?
docs.text: Create a Windows Task Scheduler task that runs wsl.exe -d Ubuntu-24.04 -e sleep infinity at startup, or ensure the Hermes systemd service has Restart=always.

docs.title: Skill Template
docs.text:
Create a SKILL.md file with this structure:

---
name: your-skill-name
description: Use when X happens. One line, 60 characters or fewer.
version: 1.0.0
platforms: [macos, linux]

metadata:
  hermes:
    tags: [your-tag, another-tag]
    category: your-category
---

# Your Skill Title

Brief overview of what this skill covers.

## When to Use

- When the user asks about X
- When working with Y

## Procedure

1. First step with exact command
2. Second step with verification

## Pitfalls

- Common mistake and how to avoid it
- Another pitfall to watch for

## Verification

- Command that proves the step worked

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
How to confirm everything works:

your-verification-command

docs.title: Config Template
docs.text:
Minimal config.yaml for a new Hermes Agent setup:

model:
  default: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5
  provider: openrouter

platform_toolsets:
  cli: [hermes-cli]

memory:
  memory_enabled: true
  user_profile_enabled: true

platform_toolsets picks the tool surface per platform: a preset like hermes-cli, or your own list of toolsets (cli: [web, terminal, file, skills, todo]). hermes tools enable and hermes tools disable write this key for you.

docs.title: Cron Template
docs.text:
Schedule recurring tasks with hermes cron create. The schedule and the prompt are positional arguments, not flags:

# Daily at 9 AM
hermes cron create "0 9 * * *" \
  "Generate the daily activity report and email it" \
  --name "daily-report" \
  --deliver local

--deliver accepts origin, local, telegram, discord, signal, platform:chat_id, bot-chat[:profile], or room:<room_id>[@profile]. To run the job under a different profile, set the profile for that invocation with HERMES_PROFILE=default hermes cron create ..., or change the sticky default with hermes profile use default. Add --skill <name> (repeatable) to attach skills, or --script <file> --no-agent for a script-only job that never wakes the model.

More templates are added regularly from the Hermes community.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Guide
docs.text:
Production agent systems fail in predictable ways. This guide catalogs the most common failure modes across the Hermes stack and provides clear resolution paths.

Each section includes symptoms, diagnosis steps, and fixes - organized from most likely to least likely cause.

docs.title: MCP Connection Issues
docs.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers are the bridge between Hermes and external tools. When they fail, agents lose their capabilities silently.

docs.title: Symptom: Agent reports "Tool not available" or "MCP server unreachable"
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Check which MCP servers are running
hermes mcp list

# Check specific server health
hermes mcp test corpusiq

# Check if the MCP server process is alive
ps aux | grep mcp

Common causes and fixes:

Cause Diagnosis Fix MCP server process crashed hermes mcp list shows status "offline" Restart with hermes gateway restart, then re-run hermes mcp test <server> Port conflict Server starts then immediately exits Check lsof -i :<port>, change port in config Python dependency conflict Server fails to import modules Check pip list in the MCP server's venv, resolve conflicts Memory exhaustion Server runs but times out on requests Check htop, increase swap or reduce concurrent connections Configuration changed Server starts but tools return errors hermes mcp test <server>, and hermes mcp configure to re-check which tools are enabled

docs.title: Symptom: Intermittent tool failures ("sometimes works, sometimes doesn't")
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Check MCP server logs for timeout patterns
hermes logs agent -n 100 | grep -i "timeout\|mcp\|error"

# Check network latency to MCP server
ping -c 10 <mcp-server-host>

Common causes: - Network instability: MCP server on a different node with intermittent connectivity - Rate limiting: External API the MCP server calls is rate-limiting - Connection pool exhaustion: Too many concurrent agent threads exhausting MCP connection pool

Fix: Raise the timeouts on that server's own entry in config.yaml - timeout bounds each tool call and connect_timeout bounds the initial connection and the MCP initialize handshake. There is no global mcp_timeout key; timeouts are per server. Then let transient failures retry with backoff rather than retrying in a tight loop.

docs.title: Symptom: Specific tool always fails while others work
docs.text:
This usually means the tool's API credential is expired, its schema changed, or its external service is down.

# Test the server connection in isolation
hermes mcp test corpusiq

# Check credential status
hermes auth status google_ads

docs.title: OAuth Token Expiry
docs.text: Token management is the most common operational issue in autonomous systems. Every external service uses OAuth, and tokens expire.

docs.title: Symptom: "401 Unauthorized" or "Authentication required" on previously working tools
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Check all connector auth states
hermes connectors list
hermes connectors accounts

# Check when a specific provider credential expires
hermes auth list
hermes auth status <provider>

docs.title: Token Lifecycle Management
docs.text: Stage Action Timing Token issued Store refresh token securely Immediately 80% of TTL Proactive refresh attempt ~48h before expiry for most services Token expired Auto-refresh fails, connector enters degraded mode Immediately on 401 Refresh token expired Requires full re-auth Typically 6 months for Google, varies Re-auth completed New tokens stored, connector restored Within minutes if automated

docs.title: Automated Re-Auth
docs.text:
There is no separate token-management config file. Credentials live in ~/.hermes/auth.json (per-provider entries plus the credential_pool), and Hermes refreshes them from that store: an expired access token is refreshed with its refresh token on the next call, and a pool entry that hits a rate limit or auth failure is demoted and cooled down automatically.

To refresh on a schedule instead of waiting for the next failing request, drive the same command from a Hermes cron job:

hermes auth refresh openrouter      # refresh the pooled credential and clear its cooldown
hermes auth status openrouter       # confirm the new expiry

# cron: refresh the pooled credential before it expires
hermes cron create "0 4 * * *" \
  "Run: hermes auth refresh openrouter. Report only if it fails." \
  --name token-refresh

A refresh token that has itself expired cannot be refreshed - that needs a fresh hermes auth add <provider> round trip.

docs.title: Manual Token Reset
docs.text:
When automated refresh fails, reset the credential path:

# Clear exhaustion state for a provider's pooled credentials
hermes auth reset <provider>

# Refresh a pooled OAuth credential and clear its cooldown
hermes auth refresh <provider>

# Re-authenticate one OAuth MCP server (or every server with --all)
hermes mcp reauth corpusiq

# This runs the re-auth flow - complete it in the browser
# After re-auth, verify
hermes mcp test corpusiq

docs.title: Common OAuth Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Wrong Google account: OAuth flow defaults to the browser's logged-in account. Use incognito mode for re-auth.
  • Scope changes: If you added new Google API scopes, existing tokens don't include them. Full re-auth required.
  • Refresh token revocation: Google revokes refresh tokens after 6 months of non-use. Keep connectors active.
  • Rate limit on token endpoint: Aggressive refresh can hit OAuth provider rate limits. Space refreshes out.

docs.title: Cron Failures
docs.text: Scheduled processes are critical. When they fail silently, days of content or data can be lost before anyone notices.

docs.title: Symptom: Cron job reports success but didn't execute
docs.text:
The most dangerous failure mode. Cron tracks process exit, not outcome.

Diagnosis:

# List recent cron executions with actual output
hermes cron runs --limit 20

# Check a specific job's full execution log
hermes cron runs --limit 5 <job_id>

# Look for jobs that "succeeded" but produced no output
hermes cron runs --limit 50 | grep "status: ok" | grep "output_lines: 0"

Fix: Every cron job must include an outcome validation step:

# Bad: Just tracks exit code
def my_cron_job():
    result = do_something()
    # If do_something() returned None due to an error it caught,
    # cron sees exit 0 and marks success

# Good: Validates actual output
def my_cron_job():
    result = do_something()
    if not result or not result.get("success"):
        raise CronFailureError("Job produced no valid output")
    return result

docs.title: Symptom: Job skipped silently
docs.text:
Causes: 1. Concurrency cap: Another instance of the same job is still running 2. Rate limit: The job's external service hit a rate limit and the job backed off 3. Resource constraint: Not enough memory/CPU to start the job

Diagnosis:

# Check whether a job is still running
hermes cron status

# Check system resources at scheduled time
journalctl --since "2026-06-16 03:00" --until "2026-06-16 03:05" | grep -i "memory\|oom"

# Check rate limit logs
hermes cron runs --limit 20 <job_id> | grep -i "rate_limit\|backoff"

Fix: There is no per-job concurrency policy to set. A job that is still mid-run when its next occurrence comes due is refused with "already running" instead of double-firing, so the fix is to make the job finish inside its own period: shrink the work, raise the interval, or move long work to a --script job that exits fast. Confirm the overlap in the run history before changing anything:

hermes cron runs --limit 20 <job_id>     # look for back-to-back runs with no gap
hermes cron edit <job_id>                # widen the schedule if runs are colliding

docs.title: Symptom: Upstream dependency failed (context_from chain broken)
docs.text:
Jobs that depend on other jobs (context_from) fail when the upstream fails.

Fix: context_from takes one job id or a list of them, nothing else - there is no primary:/fallback:/max_staleness_hours: mapping. List the upstream jobs in priority order so the second one covers when the first has no output, and check the upstream job's own state before blaming the chain:

context_from: ["daily_data_sync", "daily_data_sync_cached"]

Outputs are concatenated in the order listed, silent ticks and empty outputs are skipped when the context is assembled, and error documents stay eligible so the next run still gets recovery context. If the upstream really is stale, hermes cron runs --limit 5 <job_id> reports last_error / last_fire_error for it - fix that job rather than teaching the consumer to guess.

docs.title: Cron Monitoring Setup
docs.text:
There is no separate cron monitor config file and no alert_channel: key. Jobs live in one flat ~/.hermes/cron/jobs.json table, so the monitor is itself a cron job - a no-agent script job whose only job is to look at the others:

# Script is a file under $HERMES_HOME/scripts/, never a command line
hermes cron create "*/15 * * * *" \
  --no-agent \
  --script cron-health.sh \
  --name cron-health \
  --deliver local

The script prints nothing while every job's last_status is ok (empty stdout is a silent tick, so a healthy fleet stays quiet) and prints one line per problem job. A non-zero exit or a timeout raises its own alert, so a broken watchdog cannot fail silently. hermes cron doctor runs the built-in consistency checks over the same table, and --failure-deliver keeps failure notices pointed at a channel that survives when a job's normal delivery target is broken.

docs.title: Browser Automation Failures
docs.text: Browser automation is inherently fragile. Websites change, CAPTCHAs appear, and network conditions vary.

docs.title: Symptom: "Browser executable doesn't exist"
docs.text:
Diagnosis: Hermes picks the first Chromium that exists, in this order: browser.executable_path in config.yaml, the Chromium installed by the package manager, /etc/hermes/chromium-executable-path (official Docker image), then a system chromium / chromium-browser on PATH. agent-browser is a retired package name that now maps to chromium, so a ~/.agent-browser/config.json from an older install is not read at all.

Fix: Install or repair the packaged Chromium, then point at an explicit binary only if you need a different build:

hermes pm install chromium        # also undoes an earlier --skip-browser choice
npx playwright install-deps chromium   # Debian/Ubuntu system libraries

# ~/.hermes/config.yaml
browser:
  executable_path: ""     # "" = the packaged Chromium
  chromium_args: ["--no-sandbox", "--disable-dev-shm-usage"]
  headed: false

browser.executable_path accepts a path or a bare command name. On aarch64 Linux where no packaged build exists, install a system Chromium and leave executable_path empty so the PATH fallback finds it.

docs.title: Symptom: Browser times out on navigation
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Check if the target site is reachable
curl -I --max-time 10 https://target-site.com

# Check DNS resolution
nslookup target-site.com

Common causes: - DNS issues on worker node: Configure fallback DNS (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1) - Site uses heavy JavaScript: Increase navigation timeout to 60s - Site blocks datacenter IPs: Use residential proxy or different exit node

Fix:

# Configure browser with appropriate timeouts
browser_config = {
    "navigation_timeout": 60000,  # 60 seconds
    "action_timeout": 30000,       # 30 seconds per action
    "wait_until": "networkidle",   # Wait for network to settle
    "retry_on_timeout": true,
    "max_retries": 2
}

docs.title: Symptom: CAPTCHA or anti-bot detection
docs.text:
Diagnosis: Browser screenshot shows CAPTCHA or "unusual traffic" page.

Prevention strategies (in order of effectiveness):

  1. Persistent browser profiles: Use userDataDir so the browser has cookies, history, and appears human
  2. Stealth techniques: Enable Playwright stealth plugin to mask automation signals
  3. Human-like behavior: Add random delays (500ms-3s) between actions, vary typing speed, scroll naturally
  4. Rotating user agents: Change user agent periodically to avoid fingerprinting
  5. Residential proxies: For high-value targets, route through residential IPs

When CAPTCHA appears: The task fails and is retried. If CAPTCHA persists across 3 retries, the task is escalated for human review. The browser automation cannot solve CAPTCHAs by design - attempting to would violate most platforms' terms of service.

docs.title: Symptom: "Target closed" mid-operation
docs.text:
The page navigated away or closed unexpectedly.

Fix: Re-navigate and snapshot before interacting:

def safe_interact(url: str, action: callable):
    for attempt in range(3):
        try:
            page = browser.navigate(url)
            snapshot = browser.snapshot()  # Verify we're on the right page
            return action(page)
        except TargetClosedError:
            if attempt == 2:
                raise
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)

docs.title: Symptom: Wrong model used for task type
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Check which model was used for recent tasks
hermes insights --days 7

# Check routing rules
hermes config show

Common routing problems:

Hermes does not have a task-type routing table: the model is whatever model.default / model.provider resolve to, a per-job cron pin, or the active fallback chain. That makes every one of these a configuration question, not a rule to add:

Problem Cause Fix Premium model for simple classification The session is running the default model Set a cheaper default, or pin just that job: hermes cron edit <job_id> --model <cheap-model> Lightweight model for complex reasoning No per-task escalation exists Switch that conversation with /model, or pin a stronger model on the job that needs it Model from the wrong provider model.provider and model.default disagree Run hermes model - it writes both keys together

docs.title: Symptom: "Model not found" or provider errors
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Verify provider connection
hermes doctor
hermes auth status deepseek
hermes auth status anthropic
hermes auth status openai

# Check rate limit status
hermes usage

Fixes:

  • Provider API key expired → Re-add the credential with hermes auth add <provider>, or switch provider with hermes model
  • Rate limit hit → Implement exponential backoff in router
  • Model deprecated → Update to newer model version in config
  • Provider outage → Configure fallback provider chain

docs.title: Symptom: High token costs
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Token and cost breakdown for the last 7 days
hermes insights --days 7

# Same view filtered to one platform
hermes insights --days 7 --source cli

Optimization:

# What the last 7 days actually cost, and which sessions drove it
hermes insights --days 7

# Shrink the fixed prompt before a single token is billed
hermes prompt-size
hermes tools disable <toolset>

# Keep the scheduled fleet on a cheap model without touching your chat model
hermes config set cron.model <cheap-model>

# Cheap primary, stronger provider takes over only on failure
hermes fallback add

There is no cost_ceiling_daily or routing: block in a models.yaml - a hard spend stop is a provider-side budget on the API key, not a Hermes config key. Hermes itself gives you the per-session cost breakdown, the per-job cron model pin, and the fallback chain.

docs.title: Gateway Crashes
docs.text: The API gateway is the entry point for all agent requests. When it goes down, everything stops.

docs.title: Symptom: All requests failing with 502/503
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Check gateway process
hermes gateway status

# Check gateway logs
hermes logs gateway -n 50

# Check system resources
free -h
df -h
htop

Common causes and fixes:

Cause Diagnosis Fix Memory exhausted free -h shows 98%+ used Restart gateway, increase swap, investigate memory leak Disk full df -h shows 100% on any partition Clean logs (journalctl --vacuum-size=500M), remove temp files Port conflict Another process bound to gateway port lsof -i :<port>, kill conflicting process, restart gateway Config parse error Gateway fails to start after config change hermes config check, revert last change Upstream LLM provider down Gateway can't reach any model provider Check provider status pages, enable degraded mode with local models

docs.title: Symptom: Gateway running but requests hang
docs.text:
Diagnosis:

# Check active connections
ss -tunap | grep <gateway_port>

# Check for hung threads on the Python gateway process
py-spy dump --pid $(pgrep -f "hermes gateway")

Common causes: - Connection pool exhaustion: All connections to an upstream service are in use - Deadlock in model router: Two requests waiting on each other - Blocked event loop: A synchronous tool call holding the loop, starving every other request

Fix: Restart the gateway with hermes gateway restart. For recurring issues, tune connection pool size and move blocking work off the event loop.

docs.title: Gateway Recovery Procedure
docs.text:
# 1. Check what's wrong
hermes gateway status
hermes logs gateway -n 50

# 2. First try a graceful ensure (starts the local runtime if it is down)
hermes gateway ensure

# 3. If ensure fails, hard restart
hermes gateway restart

# 4. Verify recovery
curl -f http://localhost:<gateway_port>/health

# 5. Check all downstream services recovered
hermes status --full

# 6. Re-run the affected cron job
hermes cron run <job_id>

docs.title: Symptom: "Connection refused" to worker node
docs.text:
# Check if SSH is running on the worker
ssh user@worker-node.local "echo 'SSH is alive'"

# If not, check worker node status
ping worker-node.local

Fix path: 1. If ping works but SSH doesn't → SSH daemon stopped. Restart via out-of-band access (physical, KVM, or management interface). 2. If ping doesn't work → Network issue. Check switch, cables, Wi-Fi, firewall rules. 3. If both fail → Worker node may be powered off. Check power.

docs.title: Symptom: "Host key verification failed"
docs.text:
This usually means the worker node was re-imaged or its SSH host key changed.

# Remove the old host key
ssh-keygen -R worker-node.local

# Accept the new key
ssh user@worker-node.local

docs.title: Worker Node Health Check
docs.text:
Cron jobs are created through the CLI (or the cronjob_manage tool), not by dropping a YAML file into a directory. A worker check is a no-agent script job: the script runs on the worker-facing host and stays silent while everything is healthy.

hermes cron create "*/5 * * * *" \
  --no-agent \
  --script worker-health.sh \
  --name worker-health \
  --deliver local

Put the checks in the script itself (ssh, df, free, browser driver, queue depth) and make it exit non-zero on failure - a non-zero exit or timeout is delivered as an alert, while empty stdout is a silent tick. --failure-deliver routes those failure notices to a channel that survives when the job's normal delivery target is down.

docs.title: Quick Reference: Recovery Commands
docs.text:
# Full system health check
hermes status --full

# Restart the messaging gateway
hermes gateway restart

# Check what's consuming resources
hermes status --deep

# View recent errors across all components
hermes logs errors -n 50

# Test the project's build/test/start recipe end to end
hermes verify

# Re-run a failed cron job
hermes cron run <job_id>

docs.title: When All Else Fails
docs.text:
1. Check the logs: hermes status --full and hermes logs errors give you a system-wide view
  2. Isolate the failure: Test each component independently
  3. Check for recent changes: hermes config check and a git diff of the file at hermes config path show what changed
  4. Roll back: If a config change caused the issue, restore a known-good config (backups come from hermes backup, restored with hermes import)
  5. Escalate: Some failures genuinely need human intervention. The system is designed to degrade gracefully - individual features may fail while the core continues operating.

docs.title: CorpusIQ MCP Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common issues when connecting CorpusIQ to Hermes Agent.

docs.title: "Chat not found" or 401 errors on cron jobs
docs.text:
Symptom: Crons that use CorpusIQ fail with 401 or "Chat not found" delivery errors.

Root cause: The CorpusIQ JWT access token expires after 60 minutes. Cron jobs that run infrequently will have an expired token.

Fix: Use the refresh token flow. The server now mints a 30-day refresh token alongside the 60-minute access token. Save both from the device OAuth response. When the access token expires, POST grant_type=refresh_token to /oauth/token:

curl -X POST https://mcp2.corpusiq.io/oauth/token \
  -d "grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=<saved_value>"

For crons, refresh first, write the new access token into config.yaml, then run the one-shot:

curl -s -X POST https://mcp2.corpusiq.io/oauth/token \
  -d "grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=<saved_value>"
hermes -z "your cron task"

The wrapper around the cron owns the refresh and the config.yaml write, so the agent always starts with a valid JWT.

If you are still on an older JWT obtained before July 28, 2026, do one device OAuth reconnect to receive the refresh token.

docs.title: Tool calls return empty or "Tool execution failed"
docs.text:
Symptom: CorpusIQ tools return "Retrieved 0 results" or "Tool execution failed" even when data exists on other clients (e.g., Claude.ai).

Root cause: Tool call parameters are passed flat alongside action instead of nested inside params.

Fix: All CorpusIQ MCP tool calls must nest query parameters inside the params key:

# CORRECT
await session.call_tool("search_console_connector", {
    "action": "get_performance",
    "params": {
        "site_url": "sc-domain:corpusiq.io",
        "start_date": "2026-07-01",
        "end_date": "2026-07-28",
        "dimensions": ["query"],
        "row_limit": 10
    }
})

# WRONG - flat params silently fail
await session.call_tool("search_console_connector", {
    "action": "get_performance",
    "site_url": "sc-domain:corpusiq.io",
    ...
})

The tool inputSchema defines only action and params as properties. All query parameters go inside params.

docs.title: "mcpServer not found"
docs.text:
Symptom: Hermes reports the CorpusIQ MCP server is not found.

Fix: Verify the MCP config entry:

mcp_servers:
  corpusiq:
    url: "https://mcp2.corpusiq.io/mcp"

Run hermes mcp list to verify it's registered, and hermes mcp test corpusiq to check the connection and confirm tool discovery. Hermes derives the transport from the entry: url for a remote HTTP server, command plus args for a local stdio server.

docs.title: OAuth device link expired
docs.text:
Symptom: The device auth URL opened in browser says "link expired."

Fix: The device auth link is valid for 15 minutes. Force a fresh authorization with hermes mcp login corpusiq, then open the new link immediately.

docs.title: Tools not showing up
docs.text:
Symptom: CorpusIQ connects but no tools appear.

Fix: 1. Verify you've connected at least one business tool in the CorpusIQ dashboard 2. Tools are dynamically registered - you need an active tool connection 3. Run hermes mcp test corpusiq to confirm tool discovery, or hermes mcp configure corpusiq to review and toggle the tools Hermes exposes

docs.title: "Rate limit exceeded" on GitHub API
docs.text:
Symptom: GitHub API calls return 403 with rate limit headers.

Fix: 1. Check current rate: curl -H "Authorization: token YOUR_TOKEN" https://api.github.com/rate_limit 2. Rate limit resets at the top of each hour 3. Use authenticated requests - unauthenticated gets 60/hr, authenticated gets 5,000/hr

docs.title: Fork restriction (403 on fork)
docs.text:
Symptom: 403: "You cannot fork this repository at this time"

Root cause: GitHub anti-automation blocks on accounts that make rapid API calls.

Fixes: 1. Wait 1-2 hours - restriction auto-lifts 2. Use a different GitHub account 3. Reduce API call frequency (sub-1/sec)

More help: github.com/CorpusIQ/corpusiq-docs

docs.title: How CorpusIQ works
docs.text:
Short reads that explain what's actually happening when you ask CorpusIQ a question. No deep tech - just enough to know what you're using.

  • what-is-corpusiq.md - the elevator pitch and the problem CorpusIQ solves. Start here.
  • connectors-explained.md - what a connector is, why authentication is required, and what data flows where.
  • mcp-architecture.md - the developer deep dive: what Model Context Protocol is, how tools are named and scoped, and how to connect any MCP-compatible client to the live-data layer.
  • mcp-apps.md - interactive app views. How an MCP server returns a rendered interface inside the chat, the sandbox that makes it safe, and the four checks that separate a live view from a picture.
  • skills-explained.md - the skills engine. Why CorpusIQ answers complex questions consistently instead of randomly.
  • rate-limits-and-quotas.md - API rate limits, data freshness, and performance expectations. Read this before running production queries or dashboards.
  • reading-files-and-pdfs.md - how CorpusIQ reads the text inside your PDFs, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files in Google Drive, OneDrive, and Dropbox - and the one limit (scanned images) worth knowing.
  • privacy-and-security.md - what CorpusIQ does and does not do with your data. Read-only, encrypted, disconnect anytime.
  • metric-specs.md - declare a number once (MRR, AOV, active customers), then ask any AI client for it and get the same answer every time, with a provenance footer and cross-source drift checks.

docs.title: How does CorpusIQ work?
docs.text: You connect the business tools you already use with read-only authorization, then ask a question in your AI assistant. CorpusIQ retrieves the live numbers from those tools, applies the same metric definitions every time, and returns an answer with the source cited.

docs.title: Which AI assistants does CorpusIQ work with?
docs.text: ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity are natively supported. Any MCP compatible client can also connect to the same endpoint, so the answers follow you rather than staying inside one chat product.

docs.title: Does CorpusIQ keep my business data?
docs.text: Retrieval is read only and happens on demand. CorpusIQ does not retain raw customer files or full connector response payloads for direct MCP requests. Query text, per user tool call metadata and bounded outcome summaries stay in operational logs for up to 30 days, and optional indexed search has a separate embeddings and minimal metadata lifecycle.

docs.title: Do I need a credit card to try it?
docs.text: No. The trial runs for 30 days with no credit card. Every connector is included in the plan price, with no add-on tier.

docs.title: Why not just ask ChatGPT directly?
docs.text:
You can, and the answer will change with the wording, the session and the model. CorpusIQ fixes the retrieval and the metric definition, so the same business question returns the same number in every assistant, with a citation you can check.

docs.title: Connectors, explained
docs.text: A connector is a one-way, read-only link between CorpusIQ and one of your SaaS tools. Today there are 40+ of them. The list grows every month.

docs.title: What a connector does
docs.text:
When you authenticate a connector - say, Shopify - three things happen:

  1. You're sent to Shopify's login page (not CorpusIQ's). You sign in there, just like you would normally.
  2. Shopify shows you a consent screen listing exactly what CorpusIQ is asking permission to read: orders, products, customers, etc. You approve.
  3. Shopify hands CorpusIQ a token. CorpusIQ stores it encrypted, scoped to your account only. From then on, when you ask a question that involves Shopify, CorpusIQ uses that token to read your data.

That's it. CorpusIQ never sees your Shopify password. The token can be revoked from Shopify's admin panel at any time, or by disconnecting the connector from inside CorpusIQ.

docs.title: Why you have to authenticate
docs.text:
The alternative is screenshots. You log into Shopify, screenshot the revenue chart, paste it into Claude, and ask Claude to interpret it. You do that across ten tools and the founder's afternoon is gone.

OAuth eliminates the screenshot step. You authenticate once. After that, CorpusIQ reads the live data automatically when a question needs it.

docs.title: What "OAuth" means
docs.text:
OAuth is a standard handshake - the same one behind every "Sign in with Google" button - for letting one app read data from another without ever sharing your password. You log in directly with the vendor (Google, Shopify, QuickBooks), the vendor shows you what's being requested, and you approve. The vendor stays in control. You can revoke access from their side whenever you want.

If you've ever connected Zapier or Make to a tool, this is the same flow.

docs.title: Read-only, every time
docs.text:
CorpusIQ asks for read scopes only. It can pull your sales data; it cannot place an order. It can pull your QuickBooks P&L; it cannot create an invoice. It can read Klaviyo lists; it cannot send a campaign.

This is a deliberate product decision. Writing to vendor accounts is the single largest source of "agentic AI went wrong" stories. CorpusIQ doesn't take that risk on your behalf.

docs.title: The 40+ connectors today
docs.text:
Storefronts and finance: Shopify, QuickBooks, Amazon Seller, eBay, GunBroker.

Ad platforms: Google Ads, Meta Ads (Facebook + Instagram), TikTok.

Analytics: GA4, Search Console, Semrush, YouTube.

Email and SMS marketing: Klaviyo, Mailchimp, ActiveCampaign, Constant Contact, PostScript.

CRM and pipeline: HubSpot, LeadConnector (GoHighLevel), Calendly, Monday, Airtable, Odoo.

Productivity: Google Workspace (Drive, Gmail, Sheets, Calendar), Microsoft 365 (OneDrive, Outlook), Dropbox, Slack.

Databases: PostgreSQL, MSSQL, MongoDB, Cosmos DB.

The full per-connector setup guides are in the connector directory.

docs.title: When a connector isn't enough
docs.text: Some questions need three or four connectors at once. "What's my real CAC?" pulls from every ad platform, GA4, and Shopify or QuickBooks. You don't have to know that - the skills engine handles it. See skills-explained.md.

docs.title: When you want it off
docs.text:
Disconnect any connector from the CorpusIQ status panel. The token is removed from CorpusIQ's active connection state, which requires reauthorization before reuse. Provider-side authorization and token expiration remain governed by the provider; manage them in the provider's controls.

You can reconnect at any time. There is no penalty for switching off and back on.

docs.title: CorpusIQ MCP architecture
docs.text: This page is for developers. It explains what Model Context Protocol is, how CorpusIQ implements it, and how to connect any MCP-compatible client to CorpusIQ's live-data layer.

docs.title: What is MCP?
docs.text:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to external data sources and tools. It was introduced by Anthropic and is now supported by Claude, a growing list of third-party LLM clients, and an ecosystem of server implementations.

The short version: instead of copy-pasting data into a chat window, you run an MCP server that the AI can call like a function. The AI asks for data, the server fetches it, the AI gets structured results. No prompt engineering, no CSV uploads, no stale context.

MCP servers expose tools (callable functions with typed inputs and outputs) and optionally resources (documents or data the AI can read). CorpusIQ exposes tools only - one tool per connector action.

Official spec: https://modelcontextprotocol.io

docs.title: CorpusIQ's MCP endpoint
docs.text:
https://mcp2.corpusiq.io/mcp

This is a hosted MCP server. You do not run it locally. You point your MCP client at this URL and authenticate with your CorpusIQ credentials. CorpusIQ handles everything behind that endpoint: connector auth, rate limiting, data normalization, and the skills engine.

Transport: HTTP with Server-Sent Events (SSE) for streaming. Auth: Bearer token (your CorpusIQ JWT, obtained after sign-in).

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
Your LLM client (Claude, ChatGPT, custom agent)
        |
        | MCP protocol (JSON-RPC over HTTP/SSE)
        v
https://mcp2.corpusiq.io/mcp   <-- CorpusIQ MCP server
        |
        +-- Connector layer (40+ connectors)
        |       Shopify, QuickBooks, GA4, HubSpot, Meta Ads,
        |       Klaviyo, Stripe, Slack, Gmail, and 20+ more.
        |       Each connector holds an encrypted OAuth token
        |       scoped to your account only.
        |
        +-- Skills engine
        |       Pre-built runbooks that orchestrate multi-connector
        |       queries (e.g. "executive-snapshot" pulls from 6
        |       connectors, joins the data, and returns a unified
        |       business health summary).
        |
        +-- Canonical facts store
                User-declared business facts (pricing, team, decisions)
                that ground AI answers in stable, verified context.

docs.title: The connector layer
docs.text:
Each of CorpusIQ's 40+ connectors is an isolated module that:

  1. Holds one encrypted OAuth token per user account.
  2. Exposes a set of typed MCP tools (e.g. get_orders, list_campaigns, run_report).
  3. Translates MCP tool calls into vendor API calls, handles pagination, and normalizes the response into consistent JSON.

External-source retrieval tools are marked read-only. Write-capable connector and CorpusIQ control-plane tools are separately named and carry behavior-matched safety annotations. Provider scopes vary by connector and documented operation.

When you call a tool like get_orders, the flow is:

MCP tool call  -->  CorpusIQ connector  -->  Shopify REST API
                                         <--  JSON orders array
       structured result  <--  normalized JSON

The LLM never touches vendor credentials. The connector is the only layer that holds and uses the OAuth token.

docs.title: The skills engine
docs.text:
Some questions require more than one connector. "What is my true CAC?" requires every ad platform, GA4, and Shopify or QuickBooks - at minimum four separate API calls, with a join step.

The skills engine encodes these multi-step workflows as runbooks: ordered sequences of tool calls with join logic and presentation rules. When an LLM calls invoke_skill with a skill name like executive-snapshot, the skills engine:

  1. Calls the appropriate connectors in the correct order.
  2. Joins the results (e.g. ad spend by date + Shopify revenue by date).
  3. Returns a unified, structured result to the LLM.

Skills are the main reason CorpusIQ answers broad business questions better than a raw tool list. The LLM doesn't have to figure out which five connectors to call and how to join them - the runbook already knows.

Available skills include:

  • executive-snapshot - business health across finance, sales, and marketing.
  • ad-spend-truth-report - cross-platform ROAS from actual revenue data.
  • financial-command-center - cash, AR, expenses, anomalies.
  • ecommerce-command-center - store health, LTV, CAC, inventory.
  • email-lifecycle-intel - email channel health across all ESPs.
  • board-update-drafter - investor-update format from live actuals.
  • customer-health-scorecard - per-account health scoring.

Call invoke_skill or list_skills to discover and run them.

docs.title: The canonical facts store
docs.text:
CorpusIQ includes a small key-value store for user-declared facts: pricing, team composition, product positioning, past decisions. These are written explicitly by the user (not inferred), and the AI reads them at the start of business questions to ground its answers.

MCP tools: canonical_context_get, canonical_facts_get, canonical_facts_set, canonical_decisions_add.

This is CorpusIQ's answer to the "the AI doesn't know my business" problem. Instead of embedding documents, you declare facts once and they persist across sessions.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
• Operation-level permissions. Retrieval tools are marked read-only; write-capable connector and CorpusIQ control-plane tools are separately named and annotated.
  • Per-user token isolation. OAuth tokens are stored encrypted and scoped per user account. One user's token cannot be used by another.
  • Scoped direct-MCP retention. Each tool call fetches live vendor data. CorpusIQ does not retain raw customer files or full connector response payloads; operational logs retain query text, per-user tool-call metadata, and bounded outcome summaries for up to 30 days. Optional indexed search has a separate embeddings and minimal-metadata lifecycle.
  • Revocable at any time. Disconnecting a connector commits a durable inactive state before credential cleanup. Cleanup failures are surfaced for retry rather than reported as successful deletion. You can also revoke from the vendor's side (Shopify admin, Google account settings, etc.).

docs.title: Connecting Claude Desktop
docs.text:
Claude Desktop supports MCP servers natively via claude_desktop_config.json.

Add CorpusIQ as a remote server:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "corpusiq": {
      "type": "sse",
      "url": "https://mcp2.corpusiq.io/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_CORPUSIQ_JWT"
      }
    }
  }
}

Replace YOUR_CORPUSIQ_JWT with the token from your CorpusIQ account settings. After saving the file and restarting Claude Desktop, the CorpusIQ tools will appear in Claude's tool list automatically.

Config file locations: - macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json - Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json

docs.title: Connecting ChatGPT
docs.text:
Two paths are supported. Custom GPT Actions are not one of them: OpenAI retires custom GPTs on December 11, 2026 (February 11, 2027 only for FedRAMP and Enterprise workspaces with an approved deferral), and custom actions do not transfer.

The CorpusIQ app in ChatGPT (fastest). Install CorpusIQ from the ChatGPT app store and authorize it on first use. The app carries the tool list, so there is no schema to import and no action to maintain.

The MCP connector (direct).

  1. In CorpusIQ, open Settings > Integrations > ChatGPT MCP. Copy the MCP server URL and personal token.
  2. In ChatGPT, open Settings > Connectors > Add MCP server.
  3. Paste the URL and token. Save.
  4. In a new chat, click the tools icon and confirm CorpusIQ is listed, then ask "list my Shopify orders from last week."

docs.title: Connecting any MCP client
docs.text:
Any client that implements the MCP specification can connect to CorpusIQ. The endpoint supports standard MCP over HTTP+SSE.

Example using the TypeScript MCP SDK:

import { Client } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js";
import { SSEClientTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/sse.js";

const transport = new SSEClientTransport(
  new URL("https://mcp2.corpusiq.io/mcp"),
  {
    requestInit: {
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CORPUSIQ_JWT}`,
      },
    },
  }
);

const client = new Client({ name: "my-agent", version: "1.0.0" }, {});
await client.connect(transport);

// List available tools
const { tools } = await client.listTools();

// Call a tool
const result = await client.callTool({
  name: "get_orders",
  arguments: { limit: 50 },
});

Python MCP SDK example:

from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.sse import sse_client
import os

async with sse_client(
    "https://mcp2.corpusiq.io/mcp",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CORPUSIQ_JWT']}"}
) as (read, write):
    async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
        await session.initialize()
        tools = await session.list_tools()
        result = await session.call_tool("get_orders", {"limit": 50})

docs.title: Tool naming conventions
docs.text:
CorpusIQ tool names follow the pattern connector_action:

  • get_orders - Shopify or Amazon Seller orders.
  • list_campaigns - Meta Ads or Google Ads campaigns.
  • run_report - GA4 custom report.
  • get_profit_loss - QuickBooks P&L.
  • invoke_skill - run a multi-connector skill by name.
  • resolve_connector - discover which tools to call for a given intent.

Call resolve_connector with a plain-English intent to get back the exact tool schemas relevant to your question. This is the fastest way to explore what's available without reading every tool definition.

docs.title: Rate limits and pagination
docs.text:
CorpusIQ does not impose additional rate limits beyond the underlying vendor's own limits. Each connector respects the vendor's rate limit headers and backs off automatically.

All list tools (get_orders, list_campaigns, etc.) support limit and offset-style pagination (offset, starting_after, page_index depending on the connector). See each tool's schema for the exact parameter names.

docs.text:
